ALTER TABLE.summary: ALTER TABLE changes an existing table's definition. It supports column, constraint, schema, storage, ownership, and partition changes.
ALTER TABLE.explanation: ALTER TABLE changes an existing table. It can add, remove, rename, or change columns, constraints, indexes, storage settings, ownership, schemas, and partitions. Several compatible changes can be listed in one command.
ALTER TABLE.syntax:
ALTER TABLE [ IF EXISTS ] [ ONLY ] name [ * ] action [, ... ]
ALTER TABLE [ IF EXISTS ] [ ONLY ] name [ * ] RENAME [ COLUMN ] column_name TO new_column_name
ALTER TABLE [ IF EXISTS ] name RENAME TO new_name
ALTER TABLE [ IF EXISTS ] name SET SCHEMA new_schema
ALTER TABLE [ IF EXISTS ] name ATTACH PARTITION partition_name { FOR VALUES partition_bound_spec | DEFAULT }
ALTER TABLE [ IF EXISTS ] name DETACH PARTITION partition_name [ CONCURRENTLY | FINALIZE ]

parameters.name: IF EXISTS
parameters.description: Optional. Suppresses an error when the target table is missing; PostgreSQL issues a notice.

parameters.name: ONLY
parameters.description: Optional. Changes only the named table, not its descendants.

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: Existing table name, optionally qualified with a schema.

parameters.name: column_name
parameters.description: Column to add, remove, rename, or modify.

parameters.name: new_column_name / new_name
parameters.description: New column name or table name.

parameters.name: data_type
parameters.description: New column type, or type for an added column.

parameters.name: action
parameters.description: Operation such as ADD, DROP, ALTER COLUMN, RENAME, or SET SCHEMA.

ALTER TABLE.returns: No result value is described. The command changes the table definition and reports command status.

example.title: Several table changes
example.explanation: This adds a column, requires an existing column to contain no null values, and renames another column.

useCases.title: Add a column
useCases.scenario: Add a field to an existing table without recreating it.

useCases.title: Change column data
useCases.scenario: Change a column's type or provide a conversion expression.

useCases.title: Drop a column
useCases.scenario: Remove an obsolete field and its dependent table objects.

useCases.title: Change table layout
useCases.scenario: Move or reorganize tables and partitions.

interview.question: What does ALTER TABLE do?
interview.answer: ALTER TABLE changes the definition of an existing table. It supports operations such as adding or dropping columns, changing types, changing constraints, renaming objects, and changing table properties.
interview.followUp: What happens when several actions are supplied? PostgreSQL applies them together and uses the strictest lock required by any action.

interview.question: Does setting a default update existing rows?
interview.answer: SET DEFAULT changes the value used by later INSERT and UPDATE statements. It does not rewrite existing rows, so old rows keep their current values.
interview.followUp: How can existing values be changed? Run a separate UPDATE statement after setting the default.

interview.question: What happens when a column is dropped?
interview.answer: DROP COLUMN removes the column and automatically removes indexes and table constraints that involve it. Dependencies outside the table can require CASCADE.
interview.followUp: What does IF EXISTS change? It prevents an error when the column is absent and emits a notice instead.

keyPoints: Use ALTER TABLE to modify an existing table instead of creating a new table.
ONLY limits the change to the named table. Without it, descendant tables are included.
Many single-table actions can be combined, such as adding columns and changing several column types in one command.
When a column type changes, PostgreSQL reparses related simple indexes and table constraints for the new type.
Run ANALYZE after changing a column type because PostgreSQL removes that column's statistics.
The command normally requires ownership of the table.
Moving a table to another schema or tablespace also requires CREATE privilege there.
gotchas: Most forms take an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock. The required lock can differ by subcommand, and a list uses the strictest required lock.
Adding or changing a default does not update existing rows.
Dropping a column can require CASCADE when views or foreign keys depend on it.
Changing a column type needs USING when PostgreSQL cannot use an implicit or assignment cast.

ANALYZE.summary: ANALYZE collects table statistics and saves them in pg_statistic. The query planner uses these statistics to choose efficient plans; PostgreSQL usually runs ANALYZE automatically through autovacuum.
ANALYZE.explanation: ANALYZE samples table data and saves statistics in pg_statistic. The planner uses those statistics to estimate row counts and choose query plans. You can analyze a whole database, a table, or selected columns. PostgreSQL normally runs this automatically through autovacuum, but manual ANALYZE helps after large data changes.

parameters.name: VERBOSE [boolean]
parameters.description: Show progress messages and table statistics.

parameters.name: SKIP_LOCKED [boolean]
parameters.description: Skip relations that cannot be locked immediately; some later operations may still wait.

parameters.name: BUFFER_USAGE_LIMIT size
parameters.description: Set the memory amount used by ANALYZE. Units may be B, kB, MB, GB, or TB.

parameters.name: [ ONLY ] table_name [ * ]
parameters.description: Analyze only this table, optionally including descendants or partitions.

parameters.name: column_name [, ...]
parameters.description: Limit collection to these columns; the default is all columns.

ANALYZE.returns: No data value is returned. With VERBOSE, ANALYZE emits progress messages and table statistics.

example.title: Refresh statistics and inspect a plan
example.explanation: The first command refreshes table statistics. The second shows the chosen plan, runs the query, and reports actual row and buffer information.

useCases.title: Refresh planner statistics
useCases.scenario: A table received a large load or update.

useCases.title: Limit analysis scope
useCases.scenario: Only one table or a few columns changed substantially.

useCases.title: Support plan investigation
useCases.scenario: A query plan has poor row-count estimates.

useCases.title: Monitor command progress
useCases.scenario: An ANALYZE command is taking time or waiting.

related: ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... SET STATISTICS

interview.question: What does ANALYZE do?
interview.answer: ANALYZE collects table statistics and stores them in pg_statistic. The query planner uses these statistics to choose an execution plan.
interview.followUp: Why can estimates change after ANALYZE without data changes? The command samples rows randomly, so the collected statistics can vary slightly.

interview.question: What can ANALYZE target?
interview.answer: Without a table list, it analyzes tables and materialized views in the current database that the user may analyze. A table list limits the work, and a column list limits statistics collection to those columns.
interview.followUp: How can inheritance processing be limited? Put ONLY before the table name so child tables or partitions are not recursively analyzed.

interview.question: How does ANALYZE relate to EXPLAIN?
interview.answer: EXPLAIN shows the planner's estimated plan. EXPLAIN ANALYZE also executes the statement and adds actual timing and row counts, so it can reveal inaccurate estimates.
interview.followUp: What is a safety concern with EXPLAIN ANALYZE on writes? Because it executes the statement, data-changing statements can change data unless protected by a transaction that is rolled back.

keyPoints: ANALYZE gathers table statistics and stores them in pg_statistic for planner use.
Omitting targets analyzes eligible tables and materialized views in the current database.
You can name specific columns when only their statistics need updating.
The usual required table privilege is MAINTAIN; database owners can analyze their database's tables except shared catalogs.
The progress view reports active ANALYZE operations and their phases.
gotchas: Statistics for large tables are estimates from a random sample, so repeated runs can produce small changes.
Running ANALYZE on an empty table keeps any existing statistics instead of recording new ones.
Partitioned tables may need periodic manual ANALYZE to keep hierarchy statistics current.

array_agg.summary: array_agg collects input values, including nulls, into an array. You can control the element order with ORDER BY inside the aggregate call.
array_agg.explanation: PostgreSQL processes each input row and adds its value to an aggregate state. For array_agg, the final result is an array containing the input values, including nulls; an ORDER BY clause inside the call controls their order.
array_agg.syntax:
array_agg(anynonarray ORDER BY input_sort_columns) → anyarray
array_agg(anyarray ORDER BY input_sort_columns) → anyarray

parameters.name: anynonarray
parameters.description: Input values to collect. Scalar inputs may include nulls.

parameters.name: anyarray
parameters.description: Input arrays to concatenate. They must have matching dimensions and cannot be empty or null.

parameters.name: input_sort_columns
parameters.description: Optional expressions that define the order of collected values.

array_agg.returns: An array containing the input values, or an array one dimension higher when the inputs are arrays. With no input rows, the result is null.

example.title: Collect values into an ordered array
example.code:
SELECT array_agg(name ORDER BY name) AS names
FROM users;
example.explanation: This collects non-null user names into an array and sorts them inside the aggregate call.

useCases.title: Collect grouped values
useCases.scenario: A query needs one array containing values from many rows.

useCases.title: Build an ordered array
useCases.scenario: The application needs stable output for display or comparison.

useCases.title: Combine array inputs
useCases.scenario: Rows contain arrays that must be combined into a higher-dimensional array.

interview.question: What does array_agg do?
interview.answer: array_agg collects input values into an array, including null values. It returns null when no rows are selected.
interview.followUp: How do you make an empty input produce an empty array? Use coalesce, such as coalesce(array_agg(value), ARRAY[]::integer[]).

interview.question: How can you control the order of array_agg results?
interview.answer: Use ORDER BY inside the aggregate call, for example array_agg(name ORDER BY name). This makes the result order explicit.
interview.followUp: Why not rely only on a sorted subquery? An outer query operation, such as a join, can reorder the subquery output before aggregation.

interview.question: What happens when array_agg receives arrays?
interview.answer: The array form of array_agg concatenates input arrays into an array with one higher dimension. The input arrays must have matching dimensions and cannot be empty or null.
interview.followUp: What should you check when this form fails? Check that every input array has the same dimensionality and is neither empty nor null.

keyPoints: array_agg gathers every input value into an array, and null input values are retained.
For scalar values, its result type is an array whose element type matches the input type.
When its inputs are arrays, array_agg combines them into an array with one additional dimension.
As an aggregate, array_agg reduces the rows it receives to one result for each grouping context.
array_agg supports Partial Mode, so PostgreSQL can use it in eligible aggregate optimizations.
gotchas: array_agg does not return an empty array for an empty input. Use coalesce when an empty array is required.
Without an order clause, the array element order is not guaranteed. Put ORDER BY inside array_agg when order matters.
When aggregating arrays, every input array must have the same dimensions, and empty or null arrays are not allowed.

Autovacuum.summary: PostgreSQL uses VACUUM to maintain tables: it reuses space, refreshes planner statistics, updates visibility data, and freezes old rows. Autovacuum performs this work automatically when table activity reaches configured thresholds.
Autovacuum.explanation: PostgreSQL uses VACUUM to maintain tables. It can reuse space from changed rows, refresh planner statistics, update the visibility map, and freeze old rows. Autovacuum normally runs VACUUM and ANALYZE when table activity reaches configured thresholds. Regular VACUUM is preferred over VACUUM FULL because it can run alongside normal data operations.
Autovacuum.syntax:
VACUUM [ ( option [, ...] ) ] [ table_and_columns [, ...] ]
ANALYZE [ ( option [, ...] ) ] [ table_and_columns [, ...] ]

parameters.name: autovacuum
parameters.description: Enables the autovacuum launcher. It is on by default.

parameters.name: autovacuum_max_workers
parameters.description: Maximum number of autovacuum worker processes running at once. The default is 3.

parameters.name: autovacuum_naptime
parameters.description: Minimum delay between autovacuum rounds for one database. The default is 1 minute.

parameters.name: autovacuum_vacuum_threshold
parameters.description: Minimum updated or deleted tuples that trigger VACUUM. The default is 50.

parameters.name: autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor
parameters.description: Table-size fraction added to the VACUUM threshold. The default is 0.2.

parameters.name: autovacuum_analyze_threshold
parameters.description: Minimum changed tuples that trigger ANALYZE. The default is 50.

parameters.name: autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor
parameters.description: Table-size fraction added to the ANALYZE threshold. The default is 0.1.

example.title: Run routine maintenance
example.code: VACUUM (ANALYZE) public.orders;
example.explanation: This cleans the table and updates planner statistics in one command.

useCases.title: Reuse space from changed rows
useCases.scenario: A table receives frequent updates or deletes.

useCases.title: Refresh planner statistics
useCases.scenario: Query plans become poor after data changes.

useCases.title: Maintain visibility information
useCases.scenario: A large table uses index-only scans.

useCases.title: Prevent transaction ID wraparound
useCases.scenario: A table has old transaction IDs.

interview.question: What do VACUUM and ANALYZE do?
interview.answer: VACUUM removes or reuses space from dead row versions, updates the visibility map, and freezes old rows. ANALYZE gathers statistics for the query planner.
interview.followUp: Why can index-only scans benefit? The visibility map records pages whose rows are visible to all transactions, so PostgreSQL can sometimes avoid reading the table.

interview.question: How does VACUUM FULL differ from VACUUM?
interview.answer: Standard VACUUM works while normal reads and writes continue. VACUUM FULL rewrites the table, needs an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, takes longer, and needs extra disk space during the rewrite.
interview.followUp: Why is standard VACUUM usually preferred? Frequent standard runs maintain reusable space and reduce the chance that a large rewrite will be needed.

interview.question: When does autovacuum run?
interview.answer: Autovacuum checks tables and starts VACUUM or ANALYZE when configured activity thresholds are reached. The default VACUUM threshold is 50 updated or deleted tuples plus 20 percent of table size.
interview.followUp: What happens if autovacuum is disabled? PostgreSQL still starts workers when needed to prevent transaction ID wraparound.

keyPoints: Tables need recurring maintenance; many installations can rely on the autovacuum daemon.
VACUUM maintains visibility information that can make index-only scans faster.
Autovacuum can refresh planner statistics after enough table changes.
VACUUM freezes sufficiently old rows so transaction visibility remains correct after transaction IDs wrap around.
Autovacuum waits at least one minute between examination rounds for a database by default.
The default updated-or-deleted tuple threshold for an autovacuum VACUUM is 50, before the table-size factor is added.
gotchas: VACUUM FULL blocks other operations that need the table, so use it carefully.
Turning off autovacuum does not stop safety vacuuming for transaction ID wraparound.
Returning empty pages at the end of a table to the operating system can require a strong lock.

B-tree index.summary: A PostgreSQL B-tree is a sorted, balanced index for data with a defined order. It supports equality, ranges, null checks, some prefix matches, and ordered scans.
B-tree index.explanation: A B-tree index stores values in sorted order in a balanced, multi-level tree. PostgreSQL can use it to find matching rows, scan ranges, check nulls, and return rows in index order. Leaf pages point to table rows, while internal pages point to lower tree levels.
B-tree index.syntax: CREATE INDEX [ IF NOT EXISTS ] name ON table [ USING btree ] ( column [ ... ] );

example.title: Create and use a B-tree index
example.explanation: The index supports the equality condition on email. PostgreSQL may choose it when it is cheaper than scanning the table.

useCases.title: Equality lookup
useCases.scenario: Find rows by an exact value, such as an account ID or email address.

useCases.title: Range filtering
useCases.scenario: Find values between two bounds, such as timestamps within a time window.

useCases.title: Ordered retrieval
useCases.scenario: Read matching rows in ascending or descending index order.

interview.question: What queries can use a B-tree index?
interview.answer: A B-tree is useful for values with a defined sort order. PostgreSQL uses it for equality, range, null checks, some prefix pattern matches, and ordered scans.
interview.followUp: Why does a hash index not replace it? A hash index supports only simple equality comparisons, while a B-tree also supports ordering and ranges.

interview.question: How is a PostgreSQL B-tree organized?
interview.answer: A leaf page contains entries that point to table rows. Internal pages contain entries that point to the next lower tree level. When a page fills, PostgreSQL splits it and may split parent pages up to the root.
interview.followUp: What happens when the root fills? PostgreSQL creates a new root above it, adding another tree level.

interview.question: What does B-tree deduplication do?
interview.answer: Deduplication combines duplicate leaf entries into a posting-list entry. The key values are stored once, followed by sorted table row identifiers, which can reduce index size and maintenance work.
interview.followUp: Is deduplication always available? It is an optional B-tree technique and is enabled by default in the documented implementation.

keyPoints: B-trees work with data types that have a clear linear sort order.
CREATE INDEX uses B-tree unless another index method is selected.
Use B-trees for equality and range conditions on sortable values.
Null checks on an indexed column can use a B-tree.
A B-tree can provide rows in index order, which may avoid a separate sort.
Leaf pages hold entries that identify rows in the table.
Internal pages direct searches toward lower tree levels.
B-tree deduplication is enabled by default and can compact repeated key values.
gotchas: A single index entry has a size limit of about one-third of a page, after applicable TOAST compression.
An ordered index scan may not be faster than reading the table and sorting the result.
A B-tree can support prefix patterns such as LIKE 'foo%', but not patterns that begin with a wildcard.

BEGIN.summary: BEGIN starts a PostgreSQL transaction block. Statements after it run together until COMMIT or ROLLBACK, instead of each statement committing separately.
BEGIN.explanation: BEGIN starts a transaction block. PostgreSQL then runs later statements in one transaction until COMMIT or ROLLBACK ends it. Without BEGIN, each successful statement normally commits by itself. A transaction block also keeps intermediate changes hidden from other sessions.

parameters.name: WORK or TRANSACTION
parameters.description: Optional keyword with no effect.

parameters.name: ISOLATION LEVEL
parameters.description: Sets the transaction isolation level: SERIALIZABLE, REPEATABLE READ, READ COMMITTED, or READ UNCOMMITTED.

parameters.name: READ WRITE or READ ONLY
parameters.description: Controls whether the transaction can write.

parameters.name: [ NOT ] DEFERRABLE
parameters.description: Controls deferrable transaction behavior.

BEGIN.returns: No result value is documented. BEGIN starts the transaction block.

example.title: Transfer changes as one transaction
example.explanation: This groups two related account changes. Use ROLLBACK instead of COMMIT to cancel them.

useCases.title: Keep related changes consistent
useCases.scenario: Run several related updates as one unit so all changes commit together or can be canceled.

useCases.title: Group multiple statements
useCases.scenario: Reduce transaction start and commit work when executing multiple statements.

useCases.title: Set transaction characteristics
useCases.scenario: Choose isolation, read/write, or deferrable behavior when starting the transaction.

useCases.title: Protect a multi-step operation
useCases.scenario: Use a transaction block before applying changes that may need a full rollback.

interview.question: What does BEGIN do?
interview.answer: BEGIN starts a transaction block. Statements after it run in one transaction until COMMIT or ROLLBACK.
interview.followUp: What happens without BEGIN? Each statement normally runs in its own transaction, with an implicit commit after success.

interview.question: Why group statements in a transaction block?
interview.answer: It lets related changes succeed or fail as one unit. Other sessions do not see the intermediate state while the transaction is open.
interview.followUp: How can you keep only part of a transaction? Use SAVEPOINT and ROLLBACK TO to discard changes after a chosen point.

interview.question: Which options can BEGIN set?
interview.answer: The command can include an isolation level, read/write mode, and deferrable mode. These options set the characteristics of the new transaction.
interview.followUp: Is BEGIN the only command for this purpose? No. START TRANSACTION has the same functionality.

keyPoints: BEGIN starts a transaction block for the statements that follow it.
Statements after BEGIN share one transaction until the block ends.
Other sessions cannot see partial changes from an open transaction.
A transaction block can reduce overhead when several statements are related.
Without BEGIN, PostgreSQL normally uses autocommit, so each statement has its own transaction.
START TRANSACTION is an alternative command with the same behavior.
gotchas: BEGIN does not finish the transaction. End the block with COMMIT or ROLLBACK.
WORK and TRANSACTION are optional words. They do not change the transaction.
Transaction modes can be separated without commas for compatibility, but commas are allowed.

BRIN index.summary: A BRIN index stores small summaries for consecutive physical page ranges. It works best when column values follow the table's physical order, helping PostgreSQL skip ranges that cannot match a query.
BRIN index.explanation: A BRIN index keeps summary data for groups of physically adjacent table pages. For ordered data, the summary can contain minimum and maximum values. During a bitmap scan, PostgreSQL uses the summary to skip ranges that cannot match, then rechecks rows because the index is lossy.
BRIN index.syntax: CREATE INDEX name ON table USING BRIN ( column ) [ WITH ( pages_per_range = number ) ];

parameters.name: pages_per_range
parameters.description: Number of table pages included in each block range. It is set when the index is created.

example.title: Create a BRIN index
example.explanation: This creates a BRIN index for a time column. The index summarizes groups of nearby table pages. The setting controls how many pages belong to each group.

useCases.title: Filter by time
useCases.scenario: A large orders table is mostly inserted in time order.

useCases.title: Filter correlated location data
useCases.scenario: Rows for nearby locations are stored near each other.

useCases.title: Keep index storage small
useCases.scenario: A table is too large for a detailed index to be practical.

interview.question: What is a BRIN index, and when is it useful?
interview.answer: BRIN means Block Range Index. It stores summaries for consecutive physical page ranges instead of storing one detailed entry for every row. It is most useful when a column's values follow the table's physical order.
interview.followUp: What happens if the column is not correlated with physical order? The summaries become less selective, so the scan may examine many table pages and provide little benefit.

interview.question: What information does a BRIN index store?
interview.answer: For data with a linear sort order, a BRIN operator class can store the minimum and maximum value in each page range. A query can use these summaries for less-than, less-than-or-equal, equality, greater-than-or-equal, and greater-than comparisons.
interview.followUp: Does every BRIN index store minimum and maximum values? No. The stored summary and supported operators depend on the operator class for the indexed column.

interview.question: Why are BRIN scans called lossy?
interview.answer: BRIN indexes support regular bitmap index scans. They are lossy: a matching range causes PostgreSQL to return tuples from all pages in that range, and the executor then rechecks the query condition.
interview.followUp: Why can BRIN still be efficient? The index is very small, so scanning it adds little overhead while allowing PostgreSQL to avoid table ranges known not to contain matches.

keyPoints: BRIN is intended for very large tables, especially when a column follows the table's physical row order.
The index divides the table into groups of physically adjacent pages and keeps summary information for each group.
BRIN indexes are small, so checking the index has low overhead compared with reading the whole table sequentially.
For linearly sortable data, each range can be summarized by its minimum and maximum column values.
The operator class determines what a BRIN index stores and which query operators it can support.
gotchas: BRIN scans can return extra rows. PostgreSQL must recheck the rows after using the index.
The pages_per_range setting affects the size of each summarized range and must be chosen when creating the index.

bytea.summary: PostgreSQL's bytea type stores variable-length raw binary data. It accepts hex and escape input; hex output is the default and is preferred for new applications.
bytea.explanation: Use bytea for raw binary data. It stores each byte, including zero and other non-printable values. Byte operations use the actual bytes, unlike text operations, which depend on locale settings. PostgreSQL accepts hex and escape input formats; hex is the default output format and is preferred for new applications.
bytea.returns: A variable-length binary string when used as a data type.

example.title: Store binary bytes
example.explanation: This creates a table, stores four bytes using hex input, and reads them with hex output.

useCases.title: Store file data
useCases.scenario: Store image, audio, or document bytes directly in a table column.

useCases.title: Store encoded bytes
useCases.scenario: Keep encrypted or compressed values without treating them as text.

useCases.title: Transfer binary data
useCases.scenario: Exchange binary values with systems that use hexadecimal representation.

interview.question: When should bytea be used instead of a character type?
interview.answer: Use bytea when the value is raw bytes rather than text. It accepts zero bytes and other byte values that character strings cannot store, and byte operations work on the bytes themselves.
interview.followUp: Why not store raw bytes in text? Text rejects zero bytes and invalid values for the selected character encoding, and its operations depend on locale settings.

interview.question: What formats does bytea support?
interview.answer: PostgreSQL accepts both hex and escape input. Hex begins with \\x and represents each byte with two hexadecimal digits; it is the preferred format for new applications.
interview.followUp: What controls output? The bytea_output setting controls it, and its default value is hex.

interview.question: How is bytea stored?
interview.answer: A bytea value is variable length. Its storage uses one or four bytes plus the binary string itself, as shown in the binary data type table.
interview.followUp: How should a client handle bytea values? It may need to escape and unescape values, depending on the front end and any character translation it performs.

keyPoints: bytea stores variable-length binary strings.
Binary values can contain zero bytes and other non-printable bytes.
Operations on bytea use byte values directly, not locale-based text rules.
Hex input uses two hexadecimal digits for each byte.
A hex bytea literal starts with \x so PostgreSQL can distinguish it from escape format.
Hex is usually a good choice for exchanging binary values with external systems.
gotchas: Output can change with bytea_output. The default is hex, but a session or system setting can select escape output.
Older PostgreSQL versions and some clients may not support hex output.
A client library may need extra escaping or unescaping, especially for line feeds and carriage returns.

coalesce.summary: COALESCE returns the first argument that is not NULL. It returns NULL only when every argument is NULL.
coalesce.explanation: COALESCE checks its arguments from left to right and returns the first value that is not NULL. It returns NULL when every argument is NULL, and it does not evaluate arguments after the value it uses.

parameters.name: value [ , ... ]
parameters.type: Expressions convertible to one common data type
parameters.description: Values checked from left to right.

coalesce.returns: The first non-NULL argument, or NULL if all arguments are NULL. The result has the common type of the arguments.

example.title: Choose the first non-NULL value
example.code:
SELECT COALESCE(description, short_description, '(none)') AS shown_description
FROM products;
example.explanation: This returns the first available description. It uses '(none)' only when both columns are NULL.

useCases.title: Fallback values
useCases.scenario: Use a preferred column when it has data, then fall back to another column.

useCases.title: Display defaults
useCases.scenario: Show a readable default instead of NULL in query output.

useCases.title: Choose available data
useCases.scenario: Pick the first available value from several optional expressions.

interview.question: What does COALESCE do?
interview.answer: COALESCE returns the first argument that is not NULL. It returns NULL only when every argument is NULL.
interview.followUp: What happens to later arguments after a non-NULL value is found? They are not evaluated, so later expressions should not be relied on for side effects.

interview.question: How does COALESCE evaluate its arguments?
interview.answer: COALESCE evaluates arguments from left to right. Once it finds a non-NULL value, it returns that value and stops evaluating the remaining arguments.
interview.followUp: Can a later invalid constant always be protected by COALESCE? No. PostgreSQL can evaluate constant subexpressions during planning in some situations.

interview.question: What type does COALESCE return?
interview.answer: Its arguments must be convertible to one common data type. That common type becomes the type of the result.
interview.followUp: How can a default value affect the result type? A literal or expression used as the default can cause PostgreSQL to choose a common type different from another argument's original type.

keyPoints: COALESCE returns the first non-NULL argument.
The result is NULL when all supplied arguments are NULL.
Arguments after the first non-NULL value are not evaluated.
The result uses a common type shared by all arguments.
COALESCE provides behavior similar to NVL and IFNULL in some other database systems.
gotchas: COALESCE looks like a function, but it is a special SQL expression. Do not treat it as an ordinary function with a VARIADIC array argument.
All arguments must be compatible with one common data type.

COMMIT.summary: COMMIT ends the current transaction. Its changes become visible to other sessions and are durable if a crash occurs. AND CHAIN immediately starts another transaction with the same transaction characteristics.
COMMIT.explanation: COMMIT ends the current transaction. PostgreSQL makes its changes visible to other sessions and ensures they remain after a crash. With AND CHAIN, PostgreSQL immediately starts another transaction using the same transaction settings as the one that ended.
COMMIT.syntax: COMMIT [ WORK | TRANSACTION ] [ AND [ NO ] CHAIN ]

parameters.name: WORK
parameters.description: Optional keyword with no effect.

parameters.name: TRANSACTION

useCases.scenario: Save several related database changes as one completed unit.

interview.question: What does COMMIT do?
interview.answer: COMMIT finishes the current transaction. Its changes become visible to other sessions and are durable after a crash.
interview.followUp: How can a transaction be canceled instead? Use ROLLBACK; it cancels the transaction's changes.

interview.question: What are WORK and TRANSACTION in the COMMIT syntax?
interview.answer: WORK and TRANSACTION are optional words and do not change the command. Therefore, COMMIT, COMMIT WORK, and COMMIT TRANSACTION have the same basic effect.
interview.followUp: Which form is a PostgreSQL extension? COMMIT TRANSACTION is the extension; COMMIT itself follows the SQL standard.

interview.question: What does COMMIT AND CHAIN do?
interview.answer: AND CHAIN commits the current transaction and immediately starts a new one. The new transaction keeps the same transaction characteristics as the transaction that just ended.
interview.followUp: What happens without AND CHAIN? No new transaction starts after COMMIT.

keyPoints: COMMIT ends the active transaction.
The transaction's changes become visible to other sessions after COMMIT.
Committed changes are protected against loss from a crash.
AND CHAIN starts another transaction with the previous transaction's settings.
Without AND CHAIN, COMMIT does not start another transaction.
Use ROLLBACK when the transaction should be canceled instead of committed.
gotchas: COMMIT outside a transaction is harmless, but PostgreSQL issues a warning.
Do not use COMMIT AND CHAIN unless a transaction is active.

COPY.summary: COPY moves data between PostgreSQL tables or query results and files, programs, or the client connection. FROM imports rows; TO exports rows.
COPY.explanation: COPY transfers rows between a PostgreSQL table or query and a server-side file, a shell program, or the client connection. FROM adds rows to a table; TO writes table or query results. Options control formats, separators, null values, headers, errors, encoding, and filtering.
COPY.syntax:
COPY table_name [ ( column_name [, ...] ) ] FROM { 'filename' | PROGRAM 'command' | STDIN } [ [ WITH ] ( option [, ...] ) ] [ WHERE condition ]
COPY { table_name [ ( column_name [, ...] ) ] | ( query ) } TO { 'filename' | PROGRAM 'command' | STDOUT } [ [ WITH ] ( option [, ...] ) ]

parameters.name: table_name
parameters.description: Destination or source table, optionally schema-qualified.

parameters.name: column_name
parameters.description: Columns copied, in input or output order.

parameters.name: query
parameters.description: A parenthesized SELECT, VALUES, or data-changing command with RETURNING.

parameters.name: filename / PROGRAM / STDIN / STDOUT
parameters.description: Server-side file path, shell program, or client stream.

parameters.name: option
parameters.description: COPY options such as FORMAT, DELIMITER, NULL, HEADER, ON_ERROR, and ENCODING.

parameters.name: condition
parameters.description: Boolean expression used to select rows for COPY FROM.

COPY.returns: On success, COPY returns the command tag COPY count, where count is the number of rows copied.

example.title: Load CSV data
example.code: COPY users (id, name) FROM '/var/lib/postgresql/users.csv' WITH (FORMAT csv, HEADER true);
example.explanation: This loads CSV rows into the listed table columns. The file is read by the database server.

useCases.title: Bulk export

interview.question: What does COPY do?
interview.answer: COPY FROM reads rows from a file, program output, or STDIN and appends them to a table. COPY TO writes table rows or query results to a file, program input, or STDOUT. A final command tag reports the number of copied rows.
interview.followUp: How can a client stream data? Issue COPY with STDIN or STDOUT, then use the client library's COPY data functions until the transfer finishes.

interview.question: Where is a file named in COPY located?
interview.answer: A server-side file is opened by the PostgreSQL server, not by the client. The file must be accessible to the server process and the PostgreSQL operating-system user. COPY TO requires an absolute output path.
interview.followUp: What should a client use for a local file? Use psql's \copy, which sends COPY data through the connection and uses the client's file permissions.

interview.question: How does COPY handle bad input?
interview.answer: ON_ERROR controls conversion errors in COPY FROM. The default stop aborts the command; ignore discards bad input rows and continues. REJECT_LIMIT can cap the number of tolerated conversion errors.
interview.followUp: When is ignore valid? Only for text or CSV COPY FROM, and REJECT_LIMIT must be positive or unlimited while ignore is enabled.

keyPoints: Use COPY TO to export rows and COPY FROM to import them.
The TO form can export the result of a parenthesized query, not only a table.
A FROM column list controls input order; omitted table columns use their defaults.
Monitor active COPY operations through pg_stat_progress_copy.
The default format is text. CSV and binary are also supported.
COPY FROM can use WHERE to reject rows that do not meet a Boolean condition.
gotchas: A named file must be on the database server and accessible to the PostgreSQL operating-system user. Use psql's \copy when the file belongs to the client.
Server-side files and programs require a superuser or an appropriate server-file or program role.
PROGRAM runs through a shell. Do not place untrusted input in the command unless it is safely escaped.
ON_ERROR = ignore does not apply to binary input or COPY TO. REJECT_LIMIT also requires ON_ERROR = ignore.

Covering index.summary: An index-only scan can answer a query from an index without reading the table heap. Use INCLUDE to build a covering index, but heap access can still be needed when visibility information requires it.
Covering index.explanation: PostgreSQL indexes normally need a heap lookup for each matching row. An index-only scan can return values from the index instead, but the index type must support it and the table's visibility map must show that the relevant heap pages are all-visible. An INCLUDE clause adds payload columns that the query returns without making them part of the search key.
Covering index.syntax: CREATE [ UNIQUE ] INDEX name ON table ( key_column [, ...] ) [ INCLUDE ( payload_column [, ...] ) ];
Covering index.returns: The query result, potentially without heap access when the index and visibility conditions permit an index-only scan.

example.title: Create a covering index
example.explanation: The index stores both x and y, so PostgreSQL can answer this query from the index when the needed heap pages are marked all-visible.

useCases.title: Cover a frequent lookup
useCases.scenario: A query filters on one column and returns another column often.

useCases.title: Reduce heap reads
useCases.scenario: A table changes slowly and many heap pages are all-visible.

useCases.title: Store payload with a unique key
useCases.scenario: A unique key must remain unique while extra result columns are stored.

interview.question: What is an index-only scan?
interview.answer: An index-only scan answers a query using index entries without fetching table rows from the heap. It requires an index type that stores or can reconstruct the needed values, and it benefits when the visibility map marks many relevant heap pages all-visible.
interview.followUp: Why is the visibility map needed? PostgreSQL uses it to check row visibility without reading each heap page. If a page is not all-visible, the heap must still be visited.

interview.question: How do you create a covering index?
interview.answer: A covering index contains the columns needed by a frequent query. Search columns go in the index key, while extra returned columns can be added with INCLUDE as payload columns.
interview.followUp: Does INCLUDE affect uniqueness? No. In a unique index, uniqueness applies only to the key columns, not the included columns.

interview.question: Which index types support index-only scans?
interview.answer: B-tree indexes always support index-only scans. GiST and SP-GiST support them for some operator classes, while other index types may not support them.
interview.followUp: Can every query use an index-only scan with a suitable index? No. The planner also needs all required columns available from the index, and visibility conditions must allow avoiding heap access.

keyPoints: An index-only scan can return query data without reading the table heap.
B-tree always supports this feature; GiST and SP-GiST support it only for selected operator classes.
The index must contain the needed value or be able to rebuild it.
PostgreSQL uses the visibility map to check whether heap access can be skipped.
Use INCLUDE to store extra query columns as non-key payload.
Included columns do not participate in a unique index's uniqueness rule.
gotchas: Wide payload columns can make the index large. An index tuple that exceeds the index type's size limit can make inserts fail.
A covering index helps less when the table changes often, because PostgreSQL may still need heap access.
Index-only scans are not available for every index type. B-tree always supports them; GiST and SP-GiST support them for some operator classes.

CREATE EXTENSION.summary: CREATE EXTENSION installs an extension in the current database. It runs the extension script, records its objects, and can place them in a chosen schema.
CREATE EXTENSION.explanation: CREATE EXTENSION runs an extension's installation script and records the objects that script creates. PostgreSQL can later remove those objects together with the extension. The command can choose a schema and version, and CASCADE can install required extensions.
CREATE EXTENSION.syntax: CREATE EXTENSION [ IF NOT EXISTS ] extension_name [ WITH ] [ SCHEMA schema_name ] [ VERSION version ] [ CASCADE ]

parameters.name: IF NOT EXISTS
parameters.description: Do not error if the named extension is already installed.

parameters.name: extension_name
parameters.description: Extension name to install.

parameters.name: schema_name
parameters.description: Schema where the extension objects should be placed.

parameters.name: version
parameters.description: Version to install. Without it, PostgreSQL uses the control file's default version.

parameters.name: CASCADE
parameters.description: Install missing required extensions recursively.

example.title: Install an extension
example.code:
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS hstore
  WITH SCHEMA addons;
example.explanation: This installs the hstore extension in the addons schema. The supporting extension files must already be installed on the PostgreSQL system.

useCases.title: Enable an extension
useCases.scenario: Add a PostgreSQL-supplied module, such as hstore, to one database.

useCases.title: Choose an installation schema
useCases.scenario: Keep extension objects out of the default schema.

useCases.title: Install dependencies
useCases.scenario: Install an extension together with missing extensions it requires.

interview.question: What does CREATE EXTENSION do?
interview.answer: CREATE EXTENSION loads the extension's script and records the objects created by that script. This lets PostgreSQL treat those objects as one managed unit.
interview.followUp: What does DROP EXTENSION do? It removes the extension and its member objects, subject to dependency rules.

interview.question: How do SCHEMA and CASCADE affect installation?
interview.answer: SCHEMA chooses the target schema for the extension's objects. If it is omitted, PostgreSQL uses the current object-creation schema.
interview.followUp: What happens with CASCADE? The selected schema applies to extensions installed automatically, but their other options do not.

interview.question: Who can install a trusted extension?
interview.answer: A trusted extension may be installed by a user with CREATE privilege on the current database. The extension object belongs to that user, while its contained objects normally belong to the bootstrap superuser.
interview.followUp: Why is trusted status sensitive? A badly written trusted script could expose superuser-only abilities, so it must be written and reviewed carefully.

keyPoints: The command installs an extension only in the database where you run it.
An extension script can create related objects such as functions, types, operators, and index support methods.
PostgreSQL tracks the created objects as members of the extension.
The user running the command normally owns the extension and its created objects.
Trusted extensions can be installed by users with CREATE privilege on the database instead of requiring superuser status.
CASCADE recursively installs missing extensions required by the selected extension.
gotchas: Without IF NOT EXISTS, the command fails when that extension is already installed.
A superuser should install unreviewed extensions only in schemas where untrusted users cannot create objects.
CREATE EXTENSION cannot work until the extension control and script files are available to the server.

CREATE FUNCTION.summary: CREATE FUNCTION defines a PostgreSQL function. It specifies the function's inputs, result, implementation language, body, and optional behavior such as null handling and security.
CREATE FUNCTION.explanation: CREATE FUNCTION adds a function to a schema. The function can use SQL or another supported language, declare its input and output types, and set behavior such as null handling, volatility, security, parallel safety, cost, and configuration values.
CREATE FUNCTION.syntax: CREATE [ OR REPLACE ] FUNCTION name ( [ [ argmode ] [ argname ] argtype [ { DEFAULT | = } default_expr ] [, ...] ] ) [ RETURNS rettype | RETURNS TABLE ( column_name column_type [, ...] ) ] { LANGUAGE lang_name | TRANSFORM { FOR TYPE type_name } [, ...] | WINDOW | { IMMUTABLE | STABLE | VOLATILE } | [ NOT ] LEAKPROOF | { CALLED ON NULL INPUT | RETURNS NULL ON NULL INPUT | STRICT } | { [ EXTERNAL ] SECURITY INVOKER | [ EXTERNAL ] SECURITY DEFINER } | PARALLEL { UNSAFE | RESTRICTED | SAFE } | COST execution_cost | ROWS result_rows | SUPPORT support_function | SET configuration_parameter { TO value | = value | FROM CURRENT } | AS ' definition ' | AS ' obj_file ', ' link_symbol ' | sql_body } ...

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: The function name, optionally qualified with a schema.

parameters.name: arguments
parameters.description: Input parameters, including optional modes, names, types, and default expressions.

parameters.name: rettype
parameters.description: The function result type, or output columns when using RETURNS TABLE.

parameters.name: lang_name
parameters.description: The implementation language, such as SQL or PL/pgSQL.

parameters.name: definition
parameters.description: The function body or external implementation definition.

CREATE FUNCTION.returns: The declared return type, or the rows and columns declared by RETURNS TABLE.

example.title: Create a simple SQL function
example.code:
CREATE FUNCTION add_numbers(a integer, b integer)
RETURNS integer
LANGUAGE SQL
IMMUTABLE
RETURNS NULL ON NULL INPUT
AS $$ SELECT a + b $$;
example.explanation: This creates a SQL function that adds two integers. It returns null when either input is null.

useCases.scenario: Encapsulate reusable database logic

useCases.title: Table-valued results
useCases.scenario: Return several named output columns

useCases.scenario: Expose controlled privileged operations

interview.question: What is the difference between CREATE FUNCTION and CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION?
interview.answer: CREATE FUNCTION defines a new function. CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION creates it if missing or replaces its definition if the matching function already exists.
interview.followUp: Can replacement change input types? No. The function name and input argument types must remain unchanged.

interview.question: How does PostgreSQL identify an existing function?
interview.answer: Two functions conflict when they have the same name and input argument types in one schema. OUT parameters do not distinguish them, so they cannot be used for overloading.
interview.followUp: What can make otherwise different functions ambiguous? Default argument values can cause the same call to match more than one function.

interview.question: How should a SECURITY DEFINER function be made safer?
interview.answer: A SECURITY DEFINER function runs with the privileges of its owner. Set a safe search_path, place pg_temp last, and restrict EXECUTE instead of leaving it available to PUBLIC.
interview.followUp: Why place pg_temp last? Temporary objects are normally searched first and can otherwise mask objects that the function intends to use.

keyPoints: Use CREATE FUNCTION to define a function in the current schema, or name another schema explicitly.
PostgreSQL supports overloaded functions. The input argument types determine which function signature is distinct.
A SET clause applies a configuration value when the function starts and restores the earlier value when it exits.
For a STRICT function with a variadic argument, PostgreSQL checks whether the whole array is null, not whether individual elements are null.
RETURNS TABLE defines output columns and returns a set of rows, unlike a function that returns one composite record.
gotchas: A function may share a name with another function only when its input argument types differ. Defaults can still make calls ambiguous.
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION cannot change a function's name or input argument types. Drop and recreate it for that change.
New functions are executable by everyone unless you revoke that default privilege. Restrict security-definer functions in the same transaction.

CREATE INDEX.summary: CREATE INDEX builds an index on a table or materialized view. It can index columns or expressions and can support faster searches, sorting, partial indexes, and index-only scans.
CREATE INDEX.explanation: CREATE INDEX builds an index for a table or materialized view. PostgreSQL can index columns or expressions, and the planner may use the index to find rows faster. Options can control uniqueness, concurrent building, included columns, ordering, storage settings, and partial-index predicates.
CREATE INDEX.syntax: CREATE [ UNIQUE ] INDEX [ CONCURRENTLY ] [ [ IF NOT EXISTS ] name ] ON [ ONLY ] table_name [ USING method ] ( { column_name | ( expression ) } [ COLLATE collation ] [ opclass [ ( opclass_parameter = value [, ... ] ) ] ] [ ASC | DESC ] [ NULLS { FIRST | LAST } ] [, ...] ) [ INCLUDE ( column_name [, ...] ) ] [ NULLS [ NOT ] DISTINCT ] [ WITH ( storage_parameter [= value ] [, ...] ) ] [ TABLESPACE tablespace_name ] [ WHERE predicate ]

parameters.name: UNIQUE
parameters.description: Makes index keys unique.

parameters.name: CONCURRENTLY
parameters.description: Builds without blocking concurrent writes; it cannot run inside a transaction block.

parameters.name: IF NOT EXISTS
parameters.description: Skips an error when an object with the same name exists, and emits a notice.

parameters.name: table_name
parameters.description: The table or materialized view to index.

parameters.name: method
parameters.description: The index access method, such as btree, hash, GiST, SP-GiST, GIN, or BRIN.

parameters.name: column_name | expression
parameters.description: Indexed columns or parenthesized expressions.

parameters.name: INCLUDE
parameters.description: Extra non-key columns stored for possible index-only scans.

parameters.name: WITH
parameters.description: Storage settings for the index method.

parameters.name: WHERE predicate
parameters.description: Limits the index to rows that satisfy the condition.

parameters.name: TABLESPACE
parameters.description: The tablespace where PostgreSQL stores the index.

CREATE INDEX.returns: Creates an index, or issues a notice with IF NOT EXISTS when an index with the requested name already exists.

example.title: Create a basic index
example.code: CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users (email);
example.explanation: Creates a B-tree index on the users.email column. Queries that search or sort by email may use it.

useCases.scenario: A query often filters or sorts by a column.

useCases.title: Build with concurrent writes
useCases.scenario: A production table must stay writable during index creation.

useCases.title: Enable index-only scans
useCases.scenario: A query needs selected table values that are not search keys.

useCases.title: Create a partial index
useCases.scenario: Only rows meeting a condition should be indexed.

interview.question: What does CREATE INDEX do?
interview.answer: CREATE INDEX creates an index on a table or materialized view. The indexed key can be a column or an expression, and several key columns are possible when the access method supports them.
interview.followUp: Which methods support multicolumn indexes? The documentation lists B-tree, GiST, GIN, and BRIN.

interview.question: When should you use CONCURRENTLY?
interview.answer: CONCURRENTLY avoids locking out concurrent inserts, updates, and deletes. It takes longer because PostgreSQL performs two table scans and waits for transactions that could affect the build.
interview.followUp: Can it run inside a transaction block? No. CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot be used within one.

interview.question: What is the purpose of INCLUDE?
interview.answer: INCLUDE adds non-key columns to index entries. These columns cannot help index search conditions or uniqueness, but they can let an index-only scan return values without reading the table.
interview.followUp: What cost can included columns add? They duplicate table data, increase index size, and can make inserts fail if an index tuple exceeds the access method's size limit.

keyPoints: The command creates an index for a table or materialized view.
An index key may be a column or a parenthesized expression.
Built-in access methods include B-tree, hash, GiST, SP-GiST, GIN, and BRIN.
A WHERE predicate makes the index partial, so it covers only matching rows.
In the documented built-in methods, only B-tree supports UNIQUE indexes.
An index can contain at most 32 key and included columns.
The maintenance_work_mem setting can affect index creation speed.
gotchas: A normal build blocks inserts, updates, and deletes until it finishes. Use CONCURRENTLY when writes must continue.
A failed concurrent build can leave an invalid index. Remove or repair it before trying again.
INCLUDE accepts columns, not expressions.

CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW.summary: CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW stores the result of a query in a table-like object. PostgreSQL remembers the query so you can rebuild the stored data with REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW.
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW.explanation: PostgreSQL runs the query when it creates the materialized view and stores the result like table data. It also saves the query, so REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW can rebuild the stored result later.
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW.syntax: CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW [ IF NOT EXISTS ] table_name [ ( column_name [, ...] ) ] [ USING method ] [ WITH ( storage_parameter [= value ] [, ... ] ) ] [ TABLESPACE tablespace_name ] AS query [ WITH [ NO ] DATA ]

parameters.name: IF NOT EXISTS
parameters.description: Skip an error when an object with the same name already exists; PostgreSQL issues a notice.

parameters.name: table_name
parameters.description: Name of the new materialized view, optionally including its schema.

parameters.name: column_name
parameters.description: Optional output column names. Without them, PostgreSQL uses the query's output names.

parameters.name: method
parameters.description: Table access method for the new materialized view.

parameters.name: storage_parameter
parameters.description: Optional storage settings supported by CREATE TABLE.

parameters.name: tablespace_name
parameters.description: Tablespace where PostgreSQL creates the materialized view.

parameters.name: query
parameters.description: A SELECT, TABLE, or VALUES command used to populate the view.

parameters.name: WITH [NO] DATA
parameters.description: Choose whether to populate the view immediately. NO DATA leaves it unscannable until refresh.

example.title: Create and refresh a materialized view
example.explanation: This stores a summary query result, adds an index, and rebuilds the stored data later.

useCases.scenario: A dashboard needs grouped historical data and does not need the newest rows on every request.

useCases.title: Cache foreign data locally
useCases.scenario: A remote or foreign data source is expensive to scan repeatedly.

useCases.title: Index derived data
useCases.scenario: Users need indexes on a stored result for fast lookups.

interview.question: How is a materialized view different from a normal view?
interview.answer: A materialized view stores the result of its query. PostgreSQL can return that stored data like table data, so it does not run the underlying query for every read.
interview.followUp: When can its data become stale? It can differ from the source tables after those tables change, until REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW runs.

interview.question: How is materialized-view data updated?
interview.answer: CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW saves the defining query and initially runs it unless WITH NO DATA is specified. REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW runs the saved query again and updates the stored result.
interview.followUp: What happens after WITH NO DATA? The view is unscannable and must be refreshed before it can be queried.

interview.question: What query can CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW use?
interview.answer: The command accepts a SELECT, TABLE, or VALUES command as its query. The query runs in a security-restricted operation, and the search path is temporarily set to pg_catalog and pg_temp.
interview.followUp: What permission is required? The user needs CREATE privilege on the schema containing the materialized view.

keyPoints: The command creates a named object that stores query results.
By default, PostgreSQL fills the view during creation.
PostgreSQL keeps the defining query for later refreshes.
Reads use the stored rows rather than directly running the source query.
The stored result may be out of date, which is acceptable for some workloads.
Creating one requires CREATE permission on its schema.
gotchas: WITH NO DATA creates the object without rows. Refresh it before querying it.
Materialized views cannot be temporary.
IF NOT EXISTS does not check whether the existing object matches the requested definition.

CREATE TABLE.summary: CREATE TABLE defines a new, initially empty table. It specifies columns, data types, and optional constraints, and can also create temporary, unlogged, typed, or partitioned tables.
CREATE TABLE.explanation: CREATE TABLE defines a new table in the current database. You provide a table name, columns with data types, and optional constraints such as NOT NULL, CHECK, UNIQUE, or PRIMARY KEY.
CREATE TABLE.syntax: CREATE [ [ GLOBAL | LOCAL ] { TEMPORARY | TEMP } | UNLOGGED ] TABLE [ IF NOT EXISTS ] table_name ( [ { column_name data_type [ column_constraint [ ... ] ] | table_constraint | LIKE source_table [ like_option ... ] } [, ... ] ] ) [ INHERITS ( parent_table [, ... ] ) ] [ PARTITION BY { RANGE | LIST | HASH } ( { column_name | ( expression ) } [, ... ] ) ] [ WITH ( storage_parameter [= value ] [, ... ] ) ] [ ON COMMIT { PRESERVE ROWS | DELETE ROWS | DROP } ] [ TABLESPACE tablespace_name ]

parameters.description: Name of the new table, optionally including a schema name.

parameters.name: column_name data_type

parameters.name: PARTITION BY

interview.question: What does CREATE TABLE do?
interview.answer: CREATE TABLE creates a new, initially empty table. Its definition includes a name, column names, and data types; constraints can restrict valid inserted or updated rows.
interview.followUp: Can it create a partitioned table? Yes. Use PARTITION BY with RANGE, LIST, or HASH, then create partitions separately.

interview.question: How do column and table constraints differ?
interview.answer: A column constraint is written with a column definition and affects one column. A table constraint is separate from a column definition and can cover multiple columns.
interview.followUp: Can a single-column constraint use table syntax? Yes. The documentation says every column constraint can also be written as a table constraint.

interview.question: What is a temporary table?
interview.answer: A temporary table uses TEMP or TEMPORARY. PostgreSQL drops it at session end, or sooner when ON COMMIT DELETE ROWS or DROP is selected.
interview.followUp: Can a temporary table use a schema-qualified name? No. Temporary tables live in a special schema, so a schema name cannot be supplied.

keyPoints: Use CREATE TABLE followed by the table name and a parenthesized, comma-separated column list.
Every column definition includes a data type, such as integer, numeric, text, date, or timestamp.
Constraints control which values INSERT and UPDATE operations may store.
Creating a table also creates a composite type representing one row.
Temporary tables are found before regular tables with the same unqualified name.
PARTITION BY creates a partitioned table whose data is stored in child partitions.
gotchas: Rows have no guaranteed order unless a query explicitly sorts them.
A table can have at most 1600 columns, and practical row-size limits may reduce this.
The user who runs CREATE TABLE owns the new table.

CREATE TRIGGER.summary: CREATE TRIGGER defines a trigger that calls a user-supplied function when selected operations occur on a table, view, or foreign table. It supports timing, event, row or statement scope, and optional conditions.
CREATE TRIGGER.explanation: A trigger attaches a function to a table, view, or foreign table. PostgreSQL calls the function when the selected event occurs. You choose whether it runs before, after, or instead of the event, and whether it runs once per row or once per statement.
CREATE TRIGGER.syntax: CREATE [ OR REPLACE ] [ CONSTRAINT ] TRIGGER name { BEFORE | AFTER | INSTEAD OF } { event [ OR ... ] } ON table_name [ FROM referenced_table_name ] [ NOT DEFERRABLE | [ DEFERRABLE ] [ INITIALLY IMMEDIATE | INITIALLY DEFERRED ] ] [ REFERENCING { { OLD | NEW } TABLE [ AS ] transition_relation_name } [ ... ] ] [ FOR [ EACH ] { ROW | STATEMENT } ] [ WHEN ( condition ) ] EXECUTE { FUNCTION | PROCEDURE } function_name ( arguments )

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: Creates or replaces a trigger with this name.

parameters.name: timing
parameters.description: The trigger timing: BEFORE, AFTER, or INSTEAD OF.

parameters.name: event
parameters.description: One or more events: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, or TRUNCATE.

parameters.name: table_name
parameters.description: The table, view, or foreign table receiving the trigger.

parameters.name: level
parameters.description: Runs once per row or once per statement.

parameters.name: condition
parameters.description: Optional Boolean condition for firing the trigger.

parameters.name: function_name(arguments)
parameters.description: The trigger function name and literal arguments.

CREATE TRIGGER.returns: Creates a trigger definition. The trigger function itself must return type trigger.

example.title: Run a function when a balance changes
example.code:
CREATE OR REPLACE TRIGGER check_update
  BEFORE UPDATE OF balance ON accounts
  FOR EACH ROW
  WHEN (OLD.balance IS DISTINCT FROM NEW.balance)
  EXECUTE FUNCTION check_account_update();
example.explanation: This runs the trigger function before an account row is updated, but only when the balance value changes.

interview.question: What is a PostgreSQL trigger?
interview.answer: A trigger is a database rule that automatically calls a trigger function when a configured operation occurs. It can be attached to a table, view, or foreign table.
interview.followUp: What must the trigger function look like? It must take no declared arguments and return the trigger type.

interview.question: How do row-level and statement-level triggers differ?
interview.answer: A row trigger runs once for every affected row. A statement trigger runs once for the SQL statement, even if it affects zero rows.
interview.followUp: Can TRUNCATE use a row trigger? No. TRUNCATE triggers can only run at statement level.

interview.question: What are the trigger timing options?
interview.answer: BEFORE triggers run before the row operation, AFTER triggers run after it, and INSTEAD OF triggers replace the operation. INSTEAD OF triggers are for view operations.
interview.followUp: When can an AFTER trigger be delayed until transaction end? When it is defined as a constraint trigger.

keyPoints: Use CREATE TRIGGER to define a trigger. Use CREATE OR REPLACE TRIGGER to create one or replace an existing definition.
A trigger can belong to a table, view, or foreign table.
Choose FOR EACH ROW to run once per affected row, or FOR EACH STATEMENT to run once per statement.
TRUNCATE is a supported trigger event.
An UPDATE trigger can name columns and fire when those columns appear in the SET list.
Trigger arguments are optional string values passed to the trigger function.
gotchas: A WHEN condition cannot contain a subquery.
Although the syntax accepts FUNCTION or PROCEDURE, the target must be a function.
A statement-level trigger can run even when the statement changes no rows.
INSTEAD OF triggers are limited to views and must run for each row.

CREATE VIEW.summary: CREATE VIEW gives a query a name that can be used like a table. The view usually stores no result rows; PostgreSQL runs its query when the view is used.
CREATE VIEW.explanation: A view stores a query definition, not its result rows. PostgreSQL runs the view query when another query uses the view. Simple views can often accept INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, or MERGE operations that PostgreSQL maps to their base table.
CREATE VIEW.syntax: CREATE [ OR REPLACE ] [ TEMP | TEMPORARY ] [ RECURSIVE ] VIEW name [ ( column_name [, ...] ) ] [ WITH ( view_option_name [= view_option_value ] [, ... ] ) ] AS query [ WITH [ CASCADED | LOCAL ] CHECK OPTION ]

parameters.name: OR REPLACE
parameters.description: Replaces a view with the same name when compatible output columns are preserved.

parameters.name: TEMP / TEMPORARY
parameters.description: Creates a session-only view.

parameters.name: RECURSIVE
parameters.description: Allows a view to refer to itself through an implicit recursive query.

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: The view name, optionally qualified with a schema.

parameters.name: column_name
parameters.description: Optional output column names.

parameters.name: view_option_name = view_option_value
parameters.description: View properties such as security_invoker.

parameters.name: query
parameters.description: The SELECT, VALUES, or other query defining the view.

parameters.name: CHECK OPTION
parameters.description: Controls whether writes must satisfy this view and, for CASCADED, underlying view conditions.

example.explanation: This creates a named query and then reads it like a table.

interview.question: What is a PostgreSQL view?
interview.answer: A view is a named query that can be used like a table. It has no physical storage for its result, so PostgreSQL runs the defining query when the view is referenced.
interview.followUp: How can a view support writes? A simple automatically updatable view can map writes to its base table; an INSTEAD OF trigger or rules can handle other cases.

interview.question: What restrictions apply to CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW?
interview.answer: OR REPLACE changes an existing view definition. Its existing output columns must retain the same names, order, and data types, but additional columns can be appended.
interview.followUp: Can the replacement query change an existing column's calculation? Yes. The expressions may change as long as the existing output column contract remains compatible.

interview.question: What is the difference between LOCAL and CASCADED CHECK OPTION?
interview.answer: LOCAL CHECK OPTION checks only the current view's condition when inserting or updating through the view. CASCADED CHECK OPTION also checks applicable conditions from underlying views.
interview.followUp: What happens with an INSTEAD rule on a base relation? PostgreSQL ignores all check options in the rewritten query, including checks from automatically updatable views above that relation.

keyPoints: CREATE VIEW gives a query a reusable name.
Views can hide table details behind a stable interface for application queries.
A view name cannot conflict with another relation in the same schema.
TEMP views last only for the current database session.
Normally, base-table access uses the view owner's permissions.
security_invoker makes PostgreSQL check underlying relations using the querying user's permissions.
gotchas: A normal view does not store query results. PostgreSQL runs its query each time the view is used.
With OR REPLACE, existing columns must keep the same names, order, and types. New columns may be added only at the end.
Using SELECT * does not make later table columns appear in an existing view.
Give expressions clear names and types. Otherwise, a string expression can get an unwanted column name and type.

date_trunc.summary: date_trunc cuts a date/time value down to a chosen precision, such as hour, day, month, or year. It returns the same general value type, with smaller fields cleared.
date_trunc.explanation: date_trunc sets all fields smaller than a chosen field to zero, or to one for day and month. It accepts a timestamp, timestamp with time zone, or interval, and returns the matching type. For timestamp with time zone, truncation uses the session time zone unless you provide a time zone.

parameters.description: The precision to keep, such as hour, day, month, or year.

parameters.name: source
parameters.type: timestamp, timestamp with time zone, or interval
parameters.description: The timestamp or interval to truncate. Date and time values are cast automatically.

parameters.name: time_zone
parameters.description: Optional time zone used for timestamp with time zone input.

date_trunc.returns: A timestamp, timestamp with time zone, or interval with less significant fields truncated.

example.title: Truncate a timestamp to an hour
example.explanation: This removes the smaller time fields below the hour.

useCases.scenario: Group event records into calendar hours, days, or months.

useCases.title: Normalize timestamps
useCases.scenario: Remove seconds and smaller fields before comparing timestamps.

useCases.title: Time zone boundaries
useCases.scenario: Create midnight boundaries in a chosen zone for time zone aware timestamps.

interview.question: What does date_trunc do?
interview.answer: date_trunc removes fields below the selected precision. For example, truncating to hour changes 20:38:40 to 20:00:00.
interview.followUp: How does it handle a timestamp with time zone? It truncates in the session time zone by default, or in the supplied time zone.

interview.question: What input types can date_trunc process?
interview.answer: It accepts timestamp, timestamp with time zone, or interval input. A date is cast to timestamp, and a time is cast to interval automatically.
interview.followUp: What does it return? It returns timestamp, timestamp with time zone, or interval, matching the input category.

interview.question: When can the time_zone argument be used?
interview.answer: The optional third argument names the time zone used for truncating a timestamp with time zone. It cannot be used with timestamp without time zone or interval.
interview.followUp: Why can an explicit zone matter? Midnight and other boundaries depend on the chosen zone, especially when daylight-saving changes occur.

keyPoints: Valid fields range from microseconds through millennium. Common choices include hour, day, week, month, quarter, and year.
The result keeps the corresponding timestamp or interval type.
Smaller fields become zero, while day and month use one when they are truncated.
For timestamp with time zone, the current session TimeZone controls the default truncation zone.
A third argument lets you choose another time zone for timestamp with time zone input.
gotchas: The optional time zone argument works only with timestamp with time zone input.
The field is a text value such as hour, day, week, month, or year; it is not a SQL type name.

Deadlocks.summary: A deadlock happens when transactions wait for locks held by each other. PostgreSQL detects the cycle, aborts one transaction, and lets the others proceed.
Deadlocks.explanation: A deadlock occurs when transactions hold locks that the other transactions need, so each waits for another to finish. PostgreSQL detects the cycle and aborts one transaction; applications should retry the aborted transaction and acquire locks in a consistent order.
Deadlocks.syntax: LOCK [ TABLE ] [ ONLY ] name [ * ] [ [ AS ] alias ] [ lockmode ] [ NOWAIT ]

parameters.name: deadlock_timeout
parameters.description: Time to wait for a lock before checking for a deadlock. The default is 1 second.

parameters.name: max_locks_per_transaction
parameters.description: Average number of object locks allowed per server process or prepared transaction in the shared lock table.

Deadlocks.returns: One transaction involved in a detected deadlock is aborted; the other transaction or transactions can continue.

example.explanation: Update rows in a consistent order in every transaction. This reduces the chance that transactions wait for each other in a cycle.

useCases.title: Prevent lock cycles
useCases.scenario: Several transactions update multiple tables or rows.

useCases.title: Retry failed transactions
useCases.scenario: A transaction is aborted after PostgreSQL detects a deadlock.

useCases.title: Tune deadlock checks and logging
useCases.scenario: An application needs to diagnose lock delays.

interview.question: What is a database deadlock?
interview.answer: A deadlock is a cycle of waiting. For example, one transaction locks table A and waits for B, while another locks B and waits for A. PostgreSQL detects the cycle and aborts one transaction so the others can continue.
interview.followUp: How can an application reduce deadlocks? Acquire multiple locks in the same order in all transactions, and retry transactions that PostgreSQL aborts because of a deadlock.

interview.question: Can deadlocks happen without explicit locking?
interview.answer: Deadlocks can involve row-level locks, even when the application does not issue explicit LOCK commands. Two transactions can update different rows first and then each wait for the row locked by the other.
interview.followUp: What simple change fixes the account-transfer example? Make both transactions update the account rows in the same order.

interview.question: When does PostgreSQL check for a deadlock?
interview.answer: PostgreSQL checks for a deadlock after a lock wait reaches deadlock_timeout. The default is one second. A longer value reduces needless checks but delays reporting of real deadlocks.
interview.followUp: What setting helps investigate long lock waits? With log_lock_waits enabled, deadlock_timeout also controls when a lock-wait message is logged.

keyPoints: A deadlock needs at least two transactions that hold locks needed by each other.
PostgreSQL detects the cycle and aborts one transaction, allowing the remaining transaction or transactions to finish.
The main prevention method is to make every application acquire several locks in the same order.
Row updates can deadlock even when the application does not use explicit table locks.
If prevention is not enough, retry the complete transaction after a deadlock abort.
gotchas: Do not depend on PostgreSQL aborting a particular transaction when it finds a deadlock.
Without a detected deadlock, lock waits can continue indefinitely. Avoid keeping transactions open while waiting for user input.

DELETE.summary: DELETE removes rows that match a condition from a PostgreSQL table. Without WHERE, it removes every row in the table.
DELETE.explanation: PostgreSQL removes complete rows from the target table when the WHERE condition is true. Without WHERE, every row is removed. You can use USING or a subquery to use data from other tables, and RETURNING to output values from deleted rows.
DELETE.syntax: [ WITH [ RECURSIVE ] with_query [, ...] ] DELETE FROM [ ONLY ] table_name [ * ] [ [ AS ] alias ] [ USING from_item [, ...] ] [ WHERE condition | WHERE CURRENT OF cursor_name ] [ RETURNING [ WITH ( { OLD | NEW } AS output_alias [, ...] ) ] { * | output_expression [ [ AS ] output_name ] } [, ...] ]

parameters.name: with_query
parameters.description: Optional common table expressions used by the DELETE query.

parameters.name: table_name
parameters.description: The table from which rows are removed.

parameters.name: from_item
parameters.description: Additional table expressions available to the condition and RETURNING expressions.

parameters.name: condition
parameters.description: A Boolean expression selecting rows for deletion.

parameters.name: output_expression
parameters.description: Expressions computed and returned for each deleted row.

DELETE.returns: On success, DELETE returns DELETE count, where count is the number of rows deleted. With RETURNING, it returns the specified values for each deleted row.

example.title: Delete matching rows
example.explanation: This removes matching rows and returns the rows that were deleted.
