useCases.scenario: Remove records that match a filter.

useCases.title: Delete with related table data
useCases.scenario: Remove records based on values from another table.

useCases.title: Return deleted rows
useCases.scenario: Remove records and inspect their values in the same command.

useCases.title: Delete through a cursor
useCases.scenario: Remove the row currently selected by a cursor.

interview.question: What does DELETE do?
interview.answer: DELETE removes rows from one table when its WHERE condition is true. If WHERE is missing, it removes all rows.
interview.followUp: How can you delete rows using another table? Use USING with a join-like condition, or use a subquery in WHERE.

interview.question: What is RETURNING used for?
interview.answer: RETURNING computes and outputs values for each row that was actually deleted. Its output list works like a SELECT output list.
interview.followUp: What happens if a BEFORE DELETE trigger suppresses a deletion? The command count can be lower than the number of rows that matched.

interview.question: How can DELETE use another table?
interview.answer: USING adds table expressions whose columns can be used in the WHERE condition. The target table must not be repeated there unless creating a self-join with an alias.
interview.followUp: What is a standard alternative to USING? Use a subquery such as WHERE producer_id IN (SELECT id FROM producers ...).

keyPoints: Only rows whose WHERE expression evaluates to true are deleted.
The WHERE clause is optional, but leaving it out targets the whole table.
RETURNING can send deleted row values back to the client.
The user needs DELETE permission on the target table.
A successful command reports a DELETE count tag.
A WHERE condition must produce a Boolean result.
gotchas: A DELETE statement without WHERE removes every row. PostgreSQL does not ask for confirmation.
Use TRUNCATE when the goal is to clear the whole table and its behavior fits the task.

dense_rank.summary: dense_rank() gives the same rank to tied rows and increases the rank for each new peer group. Unlike rank(), it leaves no gaps.
dense_rank.explanation: dense_rank() assigns a rank to each row within its partition. Rows that are peers under the window ordering get the same rank. The next distinct peer group receives the next rank number, so rank values have no gaps.

example.title: Rank rows without gaps
example.explanation: This gives employees the same rank when their salaries tie. The next rank has no gap.

useCases.title: Rank items within groups
useCases.scenario: Show the salary position of each employee within their department, while giving tied salaries the same position.

useCases.title: Build tie-aware leaderboards
useCases.scenario: Create consecutive leaderboard places when several users have equal scores.

interview.question: What does dense_rank() do?
interview.answer: dense_rank() returns the rank of the current row without gaps. Rows that are peers according to the window ordering share a rank, and each peer group increases the rank by one.
interview.followUp: How does it differ from rank()? rank() leaves gaps after ties because it reflects row positions; dense_rank() counts peer groups and does not leave gaps.

interview.question: How do PARTITION BY and ORDER BY affect dense_rank()?
interview.answer: The OVER clause defines the window used by the function. PARTITION BY separates rows into groups, and ORDER BY determines peer groups and their ranking order.
interview.followUp: What happens without PARTITION BY? All input rows belong to one partition, so ranking is computed across the complete result set.

interview.question: What determines whether rows receive the same rank?
interview.answer: A peer group contains rows tied according to the window ordering. dense_rank() gives all rows in one peer group the same rank, then assigns the next consecutive rank to the next group.
interview.followUp: Can two rows have the same rank even when they have different values in other columns? Yes. Only the expressions used by the window ordering determine whether rows are peers.

keyPoints: dense_rank() returns a bigint rank for the current row.
The function advances once per peer group, so tied rows do not create gaps.
Use an OVER clause to invoke dense_rank() as a window function.
The rank corresponds to the position of the first row in the current peer group, with gaps removed.
gotchas: Use dense_rank() with an OVER clause. Calling it without OVER is not valid window-function syntax.
Rows with equal ordering values share a rank. Ranking advances once for each peer group, not once for each row.

DROP TABLE.summary: DROP TABLE removes one or more tables from PostgreSQL. Use IF EXISTS to avoid an error for a missing table; RESTRICT is the default dependency behavior.
DROP TABLE.explanation: DROP TABLE removes a table and its indexes, rules, triggers, and constraints. By default, PostgreSQL refuses the operation when other objects depend on the table; CASCADE removes those dependent objects or constraints.
DROP TABLE.syntax: DROP TABLE [ IF EXISTS ] name [, ...] [ CASCADE | RESTRICT ]

parameters.name: IF EXISTS
parameters.description: Suppresses an error when a named table is missing; PostgreSQL issues a notice.

parameters.name: name [, ...]
parameters.description: One or more table names, optionally qualified with a schema.

parameters.name: CASCADE
parameters.description: Removes dependent objects and their dependencies.

parameters.name: RESTRICT
parameters.description: Rejects the drop if dependencies exist; this is the default.

DROP TABLE.returns: No result set. The named table is removed, or the command fails when PostgreSQL rejects the operation.

example.title: Drop a table
example.code: DROP TABLE IF EXISTS app_logs CASCADE;
example.explanation: Removes the table if it exists and also removes objects that depend on it.

useCases.scenario: Remove an obsolete table and its table-owned objects.

useCases.title: Make a script repeatable
useCases.scenario: Run setup or reset scripts safely when a table may already be absent.

interview.question: What does DROP TABLE do?
interview.answer: It removes the table from the database, along with its indexes, rules, triggers, and constraints. The table itself no longer exists.
interview.followUp: What happens to dependent objects by default? PostgreSQL uses RESTRICT by default and refuses the drop when dependencies exist.

interview.question: Why use IF EXISTS?
interview.answer: IF EXISTS prevents an error when the named table is absent. PostgreSQL issues a notice instead.
interview.followUp: Can the command remove several tables? Yes. The syntax accepts a comma-separated list of table names.

interview.question: What is the difference between CASCADE and RESTRICT?
interview.answer: RESTRICT is the default and refuses the operation when dependent objects exist. CASCADE automatically removes dependent objects and objects that depend on them.
interview.followUp: Does CASCADE always remove the dependent table? No. For a foreign-key dependency, it removes the foreign-key constraint, not the other table.

keyPoints: The command deletes one or more tables from the database.
Indexes, rules, triggers, and constraints belonging to the target table are removed too.
IF EXISTS makes an absent table non-fatal and produces a notice.
CASCADE removes dependent objects, including dependencies of those objects.
RESTRICT blocks the operation when dependencies are present, and it is the default.
A table name may include its schema, such as archive.events.
gotchas: Use DELETE or TRUNCATE when you only want to remove rows. DROP TABLE destroys the table itself.
CASCADE can remove a dependent view, but for a foreign key it removes only the constraint, not the referenced table.
The command requires ownership of the table or schema, or superuser privileges.

ENUM.summary: PostgreSQL enum types define a fixed, ordered set of allowed labels. Create one with CREATE TYPE, then use it in tables and functions.
ENUM.explanation: Create an enum with CREATE TYPE and list its allowed labels in order. PostgreSQL stores the type separately, so tables and functions can use it like other data types; comparisons follow the declared label order.

parameters.name: type_name
parameters.description: The enum type name to create or use.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: A quoted label allowed by the enum. Labels are listed in sort order.

ENUM.returns: An enum type whose values are the declared labels, in declaration order.

example.title: Create and use an enum
example.explanation: This creates an enum whose values sort as sad, ok, happy, then uses it in a table and query.

useCases.title: Constrain status values
useCases.scenario: A column must accept only a small, known set of states.

useCases.title: Use declared label order
useCases.scenario: Queries need meaningful ordering for labels such as low, medium, and high.

interview.question: What is a PostgreSQL enum?
interview.answer: An enum is a type containing a fixed, ordered set of labels. Create one with CREATE TYPE, then use it in columns or function definitions.
interview.followUp: How does PostgreSQL compare enum values? It uses the order in which the labels were declared.

interview.question: How are enum values ordered?
interview.answer: The declaration order defines sorting. Standard comparison operators and related aggregate functions work with enum values.
interview.followUp: What happens if the desired order changes later? Existing values cannot be reordered; the type must be dropped and recreated.

interview.question: Can values from two enum types be compared?
interview.answer: Each enum type is separate, so PostgreSQL does not directly compare values from two enum types. Explicitly cast both values to text when label-based comparison is really needed.
interview.followUp: What is the trade-off of that cast? Text comparison uses labels rather than the enum's declared ordering.

keyPoints: An enum defines a fixed set of allowed values and gives them a defined order.
Use CREATE TYPE with ENUM and a comma-separated list of labels.
After creation, use the enum as a column or function parameter type.
You can compare enum values and use supported aggregate operations.
ALTER TYPE can add labels or rename them.
The stored representation of each enum value uses four bytes.
gotchas: Labels are case-sensitive. Spaces in labels also matter.
You can add or rename labels, but you cannot remove existing labels or reorder them without recreating the type.
Enum values from different enum types cannot be compared directly, even when their labels look the same.

EXPLAIN.summary: EXPLAIN shows PostgreSQL's chosen execution plan for a statement. It can report estimated costs and, with ANALYZE, actual execution statistics.
EXPLAIN.explanation: EXPLAIN asks PostgreSQL to show the plan chosen for a statement. The plan describes scans, joins, costs, estimated rows, and row width. ANALYZE also runs the statement and adds measured execution data, such as actual time and rows.
EXPLAIN.syntax:
EXPLAIN [ ( option [, ...] ) ] statement
EXPLAIN [ ANALYZE ] [ VERBOSE ] statement

parameters.name: VERBOSE

parameters.name: COSTS

parameters.name: SETTINGS

parameters.name: BUFFERS

parameters.name: WAL

parameters.name: TIMING

parameters.name: SUMMARY

parameters.name: FORMAT

interview.question: What does EXPLAIN do?
interview.answer: EXPLAIN displays the execution plan selected by the planner. It can show access methods, join methods, estimated costs, row counts, and row widths.
interview.followUp: What does the top-level total cost mean? It is the planner's estimated cost for completing the plan, including the costs of its child nodes.

interview.question: When would you use EXPLAIN ANALYZE?
interview.answer: EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the statement and adds actual timing and row-count information. It helps compare planner estimates with what happened during execution.
interview.followUp: Why can it be misleading for timing? Profiling adds overhead, especially for nodes that run quickly many times.

interview.question: Which output formats does EXPLAIN support?
interview.answer: The output can use TEXT, XML, JSON, or YAML. TEXT is convenient for people; JSON, XML, and YAML are easier for programs to parse.
interview.followUp: Which option can show a plan for parameter placeholders without values? GENERIC_PLAN produces a value-independent plan and cannot be combined with ANALYZE.

keyPoints: The plan can show sequential scans, index scans, bitmap scans, and other table access methods.
For multiple tables, the plan describes how PostgreSQL combines rows, such as with nested-loop or other join nodes.
With COSTS enabled, each node can include startup cost, total cost, estimated rows, and average row width.
BUFFERS reports buffer activity. It requires ANALYZE and can help show how much database-page work the plan performed.
FORMAT selects human-readable text or structured output for tools.
GENERIC_PLAN lets EXPLAIN inspect a parameterized statement without depending on particular parameter values.
gotchas: ANALYZE runs the statement. Data-changing statements can have their normal side effects, so use a transaction and roll it back when testing them.
EXPLAIN ANALYZE adds profiling overhead. Its measured time can be higher than a normal execution.
Stale table statistics can make estimates less useful. Run ANALYZE after large data changes if autovacuum has not updated them.

EXPLAIN ANALYZE.summary: EXPLAIN shows the execution plan PostgreSQL chooses for a statement. EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs it and adds actual timing and row data.
EXPLAIN ANALYZE.explanation: PostgreSQL builds a tree of plan nodes for each statement. EXPLAIN shows the chosen scans, joins, and other operations. ANALYZE executes the statement and adds measured results, so compare estimated rows with actual rows. Use machine-readable formats when another program must process the plan.

parameters.name: ANALYZE
parameters.description: Execute the statement and show measured runtime and other execution statistics.

parameters.name: VERBOSE
parameters.description: Show extra plan details, including output columns and qualified names.

parameters.name: COSTS
parameters.description: Show estimated startup cost, total cost, rows, and row width.

parameters.name: BUFFERS
parameters.description: Show buffer usage for shared, local, and temporary blocks.

parameters.name: FORMAT
parameters.description: Select TEXT, XML, JSON, or YAML output.

parameters.name: SETTINGS
parameters.description: Show planning configuration values that differ from built-in defaults.

EXPLAIN ANALYZE.returns: A textual or machine-readable execution plan. With ANALYZE, it also includes actual execution times, row counts, and other runtime statistics.

example.title: Inspect a query
example.code:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT *
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 42;
example.explanation: This runs the query and reports actual timings, row counts, and buffer activity.

useCases.title: Inspect access paths
useCases.scenario: Investigate a slow query by seeing whether PostgreSQL uses a sequential scan, index scan, or another access method.

useCases.title: Check estimates
useCases.scenario: Compare planner estimates with real execution results to find row-count estimation errors.

useCases.title: Inspect buffer usage
useCases.scenario: Measure cache and temporary block activity while investigating I/O behavior.

useCases.title: Process plan output
useCases.scenario: Export a plan for a tool or script that needs structured data.

interview.question: What does EXPLAIN show?
interview.answer: EXPLAIN displays the planner's execution plan without running the statement. The plan describes table access methods, such as sequential or index scans, and join algorithms.
interview.followUp: How would you check estimate accuracy? Use EXPLAIN ANALYZE, then compare estimated rows with actual rows and account for its profiling overhead.

interview.question: How does EXPLAIN ANALYZE differ from EXPLAIN?
interview.answer: EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the statement and reports actual time and rows for each plan node. Its actual-time values are milliseconds, while cost values are arbitrary planner units.
interview.followUp: What does loops mean? It is the total number of node executions; displayed time and rows are averages per execution, so multiply time by loops for total time.

interview.question: How is a query plan structured?
interview.answer: A plan is a tree. Scan nodes at the bottom read rows from tables or other sources, while nodes above them perform joins, aggregation, sorting, or similar work.
interview.followUp: Which output format is best for a program? Use XML, JSON, or YAML instead of the compact text format.

keyPoints: A plan is a tree of nodes. Lower nodes produce rows, and higher nodes transform or combine them.
Common scan choices include sequential scans, index scans, and bitmap index scans.
VERBOSE adds each node's output columns and more detailed names and expressions.
BUFFERS reports block activity. It can show cache hits, reads, dirty blocks, and writes.
ANALYZE can show whether sorting used memory or disk and how much space it needed.
The most useful estimate check is often the difference between planned row counts and actual row counts.
gotchas: ANALYZE runs the statement. Data-changing statements can have their normal effects. Use a transaction and roll it back when testing such statements.
EXPLAIN ANALYZE adds measurement overhead, so its runtime can be higher than the query's normal runtime.

extract.sourceTitle: PostgreSQL: Documentation: 18: 9.9. Date/Time Functions and Operators
extract.summary: EXTRACT reads a chosen part of a date, time, timestamp, or interval. It returns that part as a numeric value.
extract.explanation: EXTRACT reads one selected field from a date, time, timestamp, or interval value. The field is named after EXTRACT, and the source value follows FROM. The result type is numeric, so you can use it in calculations.

parameters.name: field
parameters.description: The field to read, such as YEAR, MONTH, HOUR, or EPOCH.

parameters.name: source
parameters.description: The date, time, timestamp, or interval value to inspect.

example.title: Get a time field
example.code: SELECT EXTRACT(HOUR FROM TIMESTAMP '2001-02-16 20:38:40') AS hour;
example.explanation: This returns 20, the hour in the timestamp.

useCases.title: Read date parts
useCases.scenario: Group or filter records by a calendar part, such as year, month, or hour.

useCases.title: Get epoch seconds
useCases.scenario: Calculate elapsed time in seconds from timestamp or interval values.

useCases.title: Number weekdays
useCases.scenario: Create weekday numbers for reports or scheduling logic.

interview.question: What does EXTRACT do?
interview.answer: EXTRACT selects a field from a date, time, timestamp, or interval. It returns a numeric value, such as the hour or month.
interview.followUp: How does EXTRACT(EPOCH ...) differ by input? For timestamptz it counts seconds from 1970-01-01 UTC; for date and timestamp it ignores time-zone and daylight-saving rules; for intervals it returns total seconds.

interview.question: What is the syntax and input?
interview.answer: The field is written between EXTRACT and FROM, as in EXTRACT(YEAR FROM some_timestamp). The source can be a date, time, timestamp, or interval, but not every field applies to every type.
interview.followUp: What happens if a field is not valid for the source type? The expression is not a valid choice because, for example, date values cannot provide fields smaller than a day.

interview.question: How do dow and isodow differ?
interview.answer: For timestamps, dow numbers Sunday as 0 through Saturday as 6. isodow numbers Monday as 1 through Sunday as 7.
interview.followUp: Why can week alone be unsafe near New Year? ISO week years can differ from Gregorian years, so use week with isoyear.

keyPoints: Use EXTRACT to read parts such as year, month, day, hour, or seconds.
The result is numeric, which makes it suitable for calculations and comparisons.
The source can be a date, time, timestamp, or interval. Time and timestamp values may include a time zone.
The field selects the part to read, such as YEAR, MONTH, HOUR, or EPOCH.
DOW uses Sunday as 0 and Saturday as 6.
ISODOW follows ISO numbering: Monday is 1 and Sunday is 7.
gotchas: With date_part, write the field as a string, such as date_part('hour', value). EXTRACT uses the field name form instead.
An epoch taken from a date or timestamp without time zone may not convert back as expected, because to_timestamp treats it as UTC.
For ISO week values near the start or end of a calendar year, also read isoyear.

gen_random_uuid.summary: gen_random_uuid() generates and returns a version 4 UUID using random data. It takes no parameters.
gen_random_uuid.explanation: Calling gen_random_uuid() creates a UUID with random data and returns it as the uuid data type. PostgreSQL sets the UUID fields required for version 4. The function takes no arguments.

example.title: Generate a random UUID
example.code: SELECT gen_random_uuid();
example.explanation: This returns one randomly generated version 4 UUID.

useCases.title: Generate row identifiers
useCases.scenario: Create an identifier for a new row when the application does not supply one.

useCases.title: Generate values in a query
useCases.scenario: Create a random UUID directly in SQL.

useCases.title: Use the core PostgreSQL function
useCases.scenario: Use a built-in function instead of installing an extension for version 4 UUIDs.

interview.question: What does gen_random_uuid() return?
interview.answer: gen_random_uuid() returns a version 4 UUID. Version 4 UUIDs are random.
interview.followUp: Which built-in function creates a time-ordered UUID? uuidv7(), which returns a version 7 UUID.

interview.question: What is the signature of gen_random_uuid()?
interview.answer: The function has no parameters. Its return type is uuid.
interview.followUp: How can a UUID version be checked? Use uuid_extract_version(uuid), which returns a smallint for supported UUID variants.

interview.question: When would you use uuid-ossp instead?
interview.answer: Use the built-in function for a random UUID. The uuid-ossp module is for additional standard UUID algorithms.
interview.followUp: What does uuidv7() provide? It generates a version 7 UUID using a time-based value plus randomness.

keyPoints: The function generates a version 4 UUID.
It takes no arguments and returns the uuid type.
Use uuid-ossp when you need other standard UUID generation algorithms.
UUID extraction functions may return null when the UUID version is not supported by that extractor.

generate_series.summary: generate_series creates a set of values from start to stop. You can choose the step and use numbers or timestamps.
generate_series.explanation: generate_series returns one row for each value from start through stop. The optional step controls the distance between values and defaults to 1. A negative step counts down. The function can generate integer, bigint, numeric, timestamp, and timestamp with time zone values.
generate_series.syntax:
generate_series(start, stop [, step])
generate_series(start timestamp, stop timestamp, step interval)
generate_series(start timestamp with time zone, stop timestamp with time zone, step interval [, timezone text])

parameters.name: start
parameters.type: integer, bigint, numeric, timestamp, or timestamp with time zone
parameters.description: First value in the series.

parameters.name: stop
parameters.type: integer, bigint, numeric, timestamp, or timestamp with time zone
parameters.description: Final boundary for the series.

parameters.name: step
parameters.description: Distance between generated values. It defaults to 1 for integer, bigint, and numeric forms.

parameters.name: timezone
parameters.description: Time zone used for time-of-day and daylight-saving calculations in the time-zone-aware form.

generate_series.returns: A set of rows containing integer, bigint, numeric, timestamp, or timestamp with time zone values, depending on the selected signature.

example.title: Generate a simple integer series
example.code: SELECT * FROM generate_series(2, 4);
example.explanation: This returns three rows: 2, 3, and 4.

useCases.title: Build a numeric range
useCases.scenario: Create rows for each integer in a range.

useCases.title: Build a time series
useCases.scenario: Create dates or times at regular intervals.

useCases.title: Expand query results
useCases.scenario: Produce rows for a query that needs a generated sequence.

interview.question: What does generate_series do?
interview.answer: generate_series is a set-returning function. It emits values from start through stop, using step between values; step defaults to 1 for integer, bigint, and numeric forms.
interview.followUp: What happens when the bounds do not match the step direction? A positive step gives no rows when start is greater than stop; a negative step gives no rows when start is less than stop.

interview.question: Which value types can it generate?
interview.answer: The integer overloads return integer or bigint values. There is also a numeric overload, plus timestamp forms that use an interval as the step.
interview.followUp: How can timestamps account for daylight-saving changes? Use the timestamp-with-time-zone form and provide its optional timezone argument, or rely on the current TimeZone setting.

interview.question: How do you generate a time series?
interview.answer: For timestamp input, step is an interval. The function includes values that reach the stop bound by repeated stepping, as shown by its timestamp examples.
interview.followUp: What if the interval is zero? A zero step is an error, just as it is for numeric series.

keyPoints: The function produces values from start to stop using the requested step.
For integer, bigint, and numeric calls, omitting step makes it 1.
Timestamp series use an interval, such as 10 hours, for step.
The time-zone-aware form accepts an optional timezone name.
In the time-zone-aware form, time-of-day and daylight-saving calculations use the named zone.
gotchas: The step cannot be zero.
Any NULL input produces no rows.
With a positive step, start must not be greater than stop. With a negative step, start must not be less than stop.

GIN index.summary: A GIN index searches for elements inside composite values, such as array members or document terms. It stores each key once and maps it to rows containing that key.
GIN index.explanation: GIN, or Generalized Inverted Index, indexes elements inside composite values such as arrays or documents. It stores each key once and links that key to the row IDs where it occurs.
GIN index.syntax: CREATE INDEX index_name ON table_name USING GIN (column_name);

example.title: Index an array column
example.explanation: This index stores array elements as keys and helps find rows whose array contains a requested value.

useCases.title: Array membership searches
useCases.scenario: Find rows containing selected array elements.

useCases.title: Document search
useCases.scenario: Search documents for words or other extracted terms.

useCases.title: Custom data types
useCases.scenario: Index custom composite data types with domain-specific operators.

interview.question: What problem does a GIN index solve?
interview.answer: GIN is an inverted index for composite values. It extracts element keys, then maps each key to the row IDs where that key appears.
interview.followUp: How does GIN handle a key found in many rows? It can use a posting list for a small set of row IDs or a posting tree for a larger set.

interview.question: How does GIN fast update work?
interview.answer: Fast update mode first puts new entries in an unsorted pending list. Vacuum, autoanalyze, an explicit cleanup, or a size limit moves those entries into the main structure.
interview.followUp: What trade-off does this create? Writes are usually faster, but searches must also scan pending entries and cleanup can make one update slow.

interview.question: How does GIN support partial matches?
interview.answer: A partial-match query supplies a lower bound instead of an exact key. GIN scans keys in order and uses the partial comparison result to stop after the possible range.
interview.followUp: What do the comparison results mean? Zero means a match, a negative value means a possible-range non-match, and a positive value means the range has ended.

keyPoints: GIN means Generalized Inverted Index.
GIN searches element keys rather than treating the whole composite value as one index value.
Repeated keys are stored once, which can keep the index compact when many rows share keys.
Each key points to the row IDs that contain it.
A multicolumn GIN index uses one B-tree whose values combine the column number and key.
GIN can search a bounded range of keys when a query does not specify an exact key.
gotchas: One row change can add many index entries, so updates may be slow.
Fast update mode can improve writes, but a large pending list can make searches slower.
For large bulk loads, rebuilding the index after loading can be faster than maintaining it during inserts.

GiST index.summary: GiST is a balanced tree framework for implementing many index strategies. Its operator class decides which operators and searches the index supports.
GiST index.explanation: GiST is a balanced tree framework for building different index strategies. An operator class defines how the index handles a data type and which operators it supports. GiST can support exact or lossy matching, and some operator classes support nearest-neighbor ordering.
GiST index.syntax: CREATE INDEX name ON table USING GIST ( column );

parameters.name: table
parameters.description: Table containing the indexed column.

parameters.name: column
parameters.description: Column whose operator class supplies the GiST indexing behavior.

GiST index.returns: Creates a GiST index on the specified table and column.

example.title: Create a GiST index
example.code: CREATE INDEX places_location_gist ON places USING GIST (location);
example.explanation: Creates a GiST index for the location column. The operators and searches it supports depend on the column's operator class.

useCases.title: Geometric data
useCases.scenario: A location column needs containment, overlap, or geometric relationship searches.

useCases.title: Nearest-neighbor search
useCases.scenario: A query must find the nearest rows to a target value.

useCases.title: Specialized data types
useCases.scenario: An application uses ranges, text similarity, or another type with a GiST operator class.

interview.question: What is a GiST index?
interview.answer: GiST is an access-method framework, not one fixed index algorithm. Operator classes use it to implement strategies such as geometric searches, range searches, and nearest-neighbor searches.
interview.followUp: What determines the operators available? The operator class determines the supported indexable and ordering operators for the indexed data type.

interview.question: What does the consistent function do?
interview.answer: The consistent support function checks whether an index entry could satisfy a query. For an internal entry it decides whether a subtree needs scanning; for a leaf it tests the indexed condition. It also reports whether the result needs rechecking.
interview.followUp: Why allow lossy results? A compact index representation can reject impossible entries while returning candidates that PostgreSQL later checks against the actual row.

interview.question: How does GiST support nearest-neighbor searches?
interview.answer: GiST can support nearest-neighbor scans when an operator class defines ordering operators and a distance function. The distance for an internal node must be the smallest distance any child could have.
interview.followUp: Why must internal-node distance be a lower bound? Returning a larger value could hide a nearer child and produce incorrect result ordering.

keyPoints: GiST means Generalized Search Tree. It is a balanced, tree-structured access method.
GiST lets domain experts add index behavior for custom data types without implementing a complete database index system.
The operator class controls which operators a GiST index can accelerate.
A GiST index is infrastructure for many possible indexing strategies, rather than one universal index structure.
An operator class needs the optional distance method to support ordered scans such as nearest-neighbor searches.
gotchas: Nearest-neighbor ordering is not available for every GiST index. The operator class must provide the needed ordering support.
A lossy GiST match is only a candidate. PostgreSQL must recheck the table row when the index cannot prove the condition exactly.
Buffered index building can use more CPU and temporary disk space. The default is usually suitable, but ordered input can sometimes benefit from disabling buffering.

GRANT.summary: GRANT gives roles privileges on database objects or makes one role a member of another. It can also control whether a member may pass on membership, inherit privileges, or switch to the granted role.
GRANT.explanation: GRANT adds object privileges to roles, or makes one role a member of another. Object privileges can apply to tables, schemas, sequences, databases, functions, and other supported objects. Role membership can also set ADMIN, INHERIT, and SET options.
GRANT.syntax:
GRANT { { SELECT | INSERT | UPDATE | DELETE | TRUNCATE | REFERENCES | TRIGGER | MAINTAIN } [, ...] | ALL [ PRIVILEGES ] } ON { [ TABLE ] table_name [, ...] | ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA schema_name [, ...] } TO role_specification [, ...] [ WITH GRANT OPTION ] [ GRANTED BY role_specification ]

GRANT role_name [, ...] TO role_specification [, ...] [ WITH { ADMIN | INHERIT | SET } { OPTION | TRUE | FALSE } ] [ GRANTED BY role_specification ]

parameters.name: privilege_or_role
parameters.description: Privileges or role names to grant.

parameters.name: object
parameters.description: Database object or schema objects receiving the grant.

parameters.name: role_specification
parameters.description: Roles, PUBLIC, or the current/session role that receives access.

parameters.name: option
parameters.description: Optional grant, membership, inheritance, or role-switching option.

GRANT.returns: No return value is described on the page.

example.title: Grant table access and role membership
example.code:
GRANT SELECT ON films TO PUBLIC;
GRANT admins TO joe;
example.explanation: The first command lets every role read the films table. The second makes joe a member of admins.

useCases.title: Grant table privileges
useCases.scenario: A reporting role needs to read application data.

useCases.title: Grant schema-wide access
useCases.scenario: Several roles need access to all tables in a schema.

useCases.title: Grant role membership
useCases.scenario: A user needs controlled access to a group of privileges.

interview.question: What are the two main purposes of GRANT?
interview.answer: GRANT has two main forms. One grants privileges on database objects, such as tables or schemas. The other grants membership in a role.
interview.followUp: How does role membership differ from object privileges? Role membership can provide access to privileges held by the granted role and can allow role changes, depending on membership options.

interview.question: Who can grant an object privilege?
interview.answer: A role can grant only privileges for which it has grant options, unless it is the object owner or a superuser. With GRANT OPTION, the recipient may grant that privilege to other roles.
interview.followUp: What happens with GRANT ALL when the issuer lacks some grant options? It grants only the privileges the issuer can grant and issues a warning.

interview.question: What do ADMIN, INHERIT, and SET control?
interview.answer: WITH ADMIN OPTION applies to role membership. It lets the member grant membership in that role to others and revoke that membership. INHERIT controls whether privileges are inherited, and SET controls whether the member can use SET ROLE.
interview.followUp: What is the default for SET on a new membership? The documentation says it defaults to TRUE.

keyPoints: GRANT adds privileges; it does not remove privileges already held by the role.
An object owner has all privileges and can pass those privileges to other roles.
ALL means every privilege available for that object type. PRIVILEGES is optional in PostgreSQL.
Some forms grant access to every supported object of a type in one or more schemas.
ADMIN on a role membership lets the member grant and revoke that role membership for others.
SET TRUE allows a member to switch to the granted role with SET ROLE.
gotchas: A table grant does not grant access to sequences used by that table. Grant sequence privileges separately.
GRANT cannot give someone the right to alter or drop an object. Ownership controls those actions.

INSERT.summary: INSERT adds one or more complete rows to a PostgreSQL table. It can use values, defaults, or a query, and ON CONFLICT can skip or update conflicting rows.
INSERT.explanation: INSERT adds one or more complete rows to a table. You can provide values, use defaults, or insert rows produced by a query; ON CONFLICT can skip a conflicting row or update it.
INSERT.syntax: [ WITH [ RECURSIVE ] with_query [, ...] ] INSERT INTO table_name [ AS alias ] [ ( column_name [, ...] ) ] [ OVERRIDING { SYSTEM | USER } VALUE ] { DEFAULT VALUES | VALUES ( { expression | DEFAULT } [, ...] ) [, ...] | query } [ ON CONFLICT [ conflict_target ] conflict_action ] [ RETURNING [ WITH ( { OLD | NEW } AS output_alias [, ...] ) ] { * | output_expression [ [ AS ] output_name ] } [, ...] ]

parameters.name: with_query
parameters.description: Optional common-table expressions referenced by the INSERT query.

parameters.name: table_name
parameters.description: The existing target table, optionally schema-qualified.

parameters.name: column_name
parameters.description: Target columns. Values map to these columns from left to right.

parameters.name: source
parameters.description: Values, DEFAULT, or a query that supplies rows.

parameters.name: conflict_action
parameters.type: ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING | DO UPDATE
parameters.description: Optional action for unique or exclusion conflicts.

parameters.name: output_expression
parameters.description: Expressions returned for each inserted or updated row.

INSERT.returns: Without RETURNING, the command tag is INSERT 0 count, where count is the number of rows inserted or updated. With RETURNING, PostgreSQL returns the selected expressions for each affected row.

example.explanation: Adds one product and returns the values from the inserted row.

useCases.title: Insert a row
useCases.scenario: Add one new record with known values.

useCases.title: Insert multiple rows
useCases.scenario: Add several records in one command.

useCases.title: Insert query results
useCases.scenario: Copy rows selected from another table or query.

useCases.title: Avoid or update conflicts
useCases.scenario: Handle duplicate keys without a separate lookup.

interview.question: What does PostgreSQL INSERT do?
interview.answer: INSERT creates rows in a table. It can take explicit values, DEFAULT VALUES, or the result of a query, and it can insert one or many rows.
interview.followUp: What happens to omitted columns? They receive their declared default values, or the type's null value when no default is defined.

interview.question: How does ON CONFLICT work?
interview.answer: ON CONFLICT chooses an alternative when a unique or exclusion constraint would fail. DO NOTHING skips the conflicting row; DO UPDATE changes the existing row.
interview.followUp: Which constraints can act as arbiters for DO UPDATE? Only non-deferrable constraints and unique indexes; exclusion constraints are not supported for DO UPDATE.

interview.question: Why use RETURNING?
interview.answer: RETURNING computes expressions from each row inserted or updated and returns them like a SELECT result. It is useful for values generated by defaults, such as sequence numbers.
interview.followUp: Can it show old and new values? Yes. RETURNING can qualify columns with OLD and NEW, including aliases declared in the RETURNING clause.

keyPoints: List target columns explicitly, and PostgreSQL matches supplied values from left to right.
Use INSERT ... SELECT to compute and insert zero, one, or many rows from a query.
RETURNING can output inserted rows or rows updated by ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE.
Inserts into a partitioned table are routed to the matching partition automatically.
For large bulk loads, COPY is usually more efficient, although it is less flexible than INSERT.
gotchas: ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE requires a conflict target. DO NOTHING can be used without one.
One INSERT with ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE cannot propose duplicate rows for the same conflict key.
RETURNING does not return a row that was locked but not updated because its conflict condition failed.

int4range.summary: int4range is PostgreSQL's built-in range type for integers. Its default form includes the lower bound and excludes the upper bound, such as [10,20).
int4range.explanation: int4range stores a range of integer values. PostgreSQL uses the range's subtype ordering to decide which values are inside it. The usual two-argument constructor creates a lower-inclusive and upper-exclusive range, such as [10,20).

parameters.name: lower
parameters.description: Lower integer bound. With the two-argument constructor, this bound is inclusive.

parameters.name: upper
parameters.description: Upper integer bound. With the two-argument constructor, this bound is exclusive.

parameters.name: bounds
parameters.description: Optional bound mode: (), (], [), or [].

int4range.returns: int4range values; range operators return boolean, while * returns an int4range intersection.

example.title: Use an integer range
example.explanation: These queries test whether a range contains a value, find the intersection of two ranges, and read the lower bound.

useCases.title: Represent an integer interval
useCases.scenario: Store integer intervals such as ID blocks or numeric limits.

useCases.title: Test containment
useCases.scenario: Check whether a value falls inside an interval.

useCases.title: Compute an intersection
useCases.scenario: Find shared values between two integer intervals.

interview.question: What does int4range represent?
interview.answer: int4range represents a range whose subtype is integer. The two-argument constructor uses [), so int4range(10,20) includes 10 but excludes 20.
interview.followUp: How would you represent a range with different boundary rules? Use the three-argument constructor, such as int4range(10,20,'(]'), where the third argument selects the bound inclusivity.

interview.question: How do you test whether a range contains a value?
interview.answer: @> tests containment. For example, int4range(2,4) @> 3 checks whether the range contains the integer 3.
interview.followUp: How can you test overlap instead? Use && between two ranges, such as int4range(3,7) && int4range(4,12).

interview.question: What is a multirange?
interview.answer: A multirange is an ordered collection of non-contiguous, non-empty, non-null ranges. PostgreSQL provides int4multirange as the multirange type corresponding to int4range.
interview.followUp: How can you expand a multirange into its parts? Apply unnest, which returns its ranges in ascending order.

keyPoints: int4range is PostgreSQL's built-in range type for integer values.
The matching multirange type is int4multirange.
A square bracket includes its boundary value. A parenthesis excludes it.
int4range(10,20) represents [10,20): 10 is included and 20 is not.
Use @> to test whether an integer belongs to an int4range value.
Use && to test whether two ranges share at least one value.
The * operator returns the values shared by two ranges.
gotchas: The + operator works only when the two ranges overlap or touch. Otherwise, the union would need more than one range.
Bound-checking functions return false for an empty range, so check isempty first when empty values are possible.

Isolation levels.summary: PostgreSQL provides four standard isolation-level names but three distinct behaviors. Read committed is the default; serializable gives the strongest protection and may require transaction retries.
Isolation levels.explanation: PostgreSQL supports four standard isolation names, but implements three different behaviors. Read uncommitted acts like read committed. Read committed takes a snapshot for each command, repeatable read keeps one snapshot for the transaction, and serializable also detects unsafe concurrent patterns and can reject a transaction.
Isolation levels.syntax: SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL { READ UNCOMMITTED | READ COMMITTED | REPEATABLE READ | SERIALIZABLE }

parameters.name: isolation_level
parameters.description: The transaction isolation mode: READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, or SERIALIZABLE.

Isolation levels.returns: No value; it changes the isolation level for the current transaction.

example.title: Request serializable isolation
example.explanation: This transaction requests serializable isolation. If PostgreSQL detects a serialization failure, the application must retry the whole transaction.

useCases.title: Default application transactions
useCases.scenario: Use read committed for ordinary transactions where each command can use the latest committed view.

useCases.title: Consistent multi-step reads
useCases.scenario: Use repeatable read when all reads in one transaction must use a stable snapshot.

useCases.title: Prevent serialization anomalies
useCases.scenario: Use serializable when concurrent transactions must produce results equivalent to some serial order.

useCases.title: Retry failed transactions
useCases.scenario: Use explicit retry handling around serializable work that may be rejected.

interview.question: What is PostgreSQL's default isolation level?
interview.answer: Read committed is PostgreSQL's default. Each SELECT sees data committed before that command started, so two commands in one transaction can see different committed data.
interview.followUp: What does repeatable read change? It uses one transaction-wide snapshot, so later reads do not see changes committed after the transaction's first non-transaction-control statement.

interview.question: How does PostgreSQL implement read uncommitted?
interview.answer: Read uncommitted is accepted as a transaction setting, but PostgreSQL treats it like read committed. PostgreSQL does not expose dirty reads through that setting.
interview.followUp: Does read committed prevent nonrepeatable and phantom reads? No. Those effects can still occur because later commands can use newer snapshots.

interview.question: What does serializable isolation guarantee?
interview.answer: Serializable is the strictest level. It makes committed concurrent transactions behave as if they ran one at a time, and PostgreSQL can raise a serialization failure when it detects an unsafe pattern.
interview.followUp: Does serializable add blocking beyond repeatable read? The documentation says its monitoring does not add blocking beyond repeatable read, but it adds monitoring overhead and may force a retry.

keyPoints: Serializable is the strictest isolation level. Its committed results must match some serial order of the transactions.
PostgreSQL accepts read uncommitted, but its behavior is the same as read committed.
Read committed is used by default unless the transaction chooses another level.
At read committed, an ordinary SELECT sees only rows committed before that SELECT began.
Repeatable read uses snapshot isolation. A transaction keeps a consistent view instead of taking a new view for every command.
PostgreSQL's repeatable read also prevents phantom reads, giving stronger protection than the SQL standard requires for that level.
Serializable monitors concurrent work for results that could not come from any one-at-a-time ordering.
gotchas: Serializable transactions can fail even when their statements are valid. The application must retry the complete transaction after a serialization failure.
Sequence changes are visible to other transactions immediately and are not undone if the transaction later aborts.
If no isolation level is selected, PostgreSQL uses read committed.

json_agg.summary: json_agg combines values from input rows into one JSON array. It includes nulls and supports ordering inside the aggregate call.
json_agg.explanation: json_agg reads one expression from each input row and places the values in a JSON array. It keeps null values, converts values using PostgreSQL's JSON conversion rules, and can order the array elements with ORDER BY inside the aggregate call.
json_agg.syntax: json_agg ( anyelement ORDER BY input_sort_columns ) → json

parameters.name: anyelement
parameters.description: One value expression evaluated for each input row.

parameters.name: input_sort_columns
parameters.description: Optional expressions that determine array element order.

json_agg.returns: json array, or NULL when there are no input rows

example.title: Aggregate values into a JSON array
example.code: SELECT json_agg(name ORDER BY name) FROM users;
example.explanation: This returns the user names as a JSON array in name order.

useCases.title: Build nested API data
useCases.scenario: Return child records grouped under each parent row as one JSON array.

useCases.title: Export query results
useCases.scenario: Convert query results into a JSON array for application code.

useCases.title: Create stable JSON output
useCases.scenario: Keep output deterministic by sorting values before aggregation.

interview.question: What does json_agg do?
interview.answer: json_agg collects every input value, including nulls, into one JSON array. PostgreSQL converts each value using its JSON conversion rules.
interview.followUp: How do you omit nulls? Use json_agg_strict, or use json_arrayagg with ABSENT ON NULL when that syntax fits the query.

interview.question: How can you make the JSON array order stable?
interview.answer: Put ORDER BY inside the aggregate call, such as json_agg(name ORDER BY name). This controls the order of elements in the resulting array.
interview.followUp: Why not rely only on a sorted subquery? Later outer processing, such as a join, can reorder the subquery output before aggregation.

interview.question: What happens when json_agg has no input rows?
interview.answer: json_agg returns NULL when it receives no rows. It does not return an empty array automatically.
interview.followUp: How can a query return an empty array instead? Apply coalesce, for example coalesce(json_agg(value), '[]'::json).

keyPoints: json_agg produces one JSON value from all rows in its input set.
Its input is one value per row, with an optional ordering expression, and its result type is json.
Null input values are retained in the resulting array.
Each input value is converted according to PostgreSQL's JSON conversion functions.
The strict variant is available when null input values should be skipped.
gotchas: For no input rows, json_agg returns NULL, not an empty JSON array. Use coalesce when an empty array is required.
Without an inner ORDER BY, the array element order is not guaranteed.
This aggregate may need to scan all rows when used over a whole table.

jsonb.summary: PostgreSQL provides json and jsonb for valid JSON values. json keeps the input text, while jsonb stores a decomposed form that is usually faster to process and can be indexed.
jsonb.explanation: PostgreSQL provides json and jsonb for valid JSON values. json keeps the input text, while jsonb stores a decomposed form that is usually faster to process and can be indexed.

parameters.name: json or jsonb value
parameters.description: The JSON value to store or process.

parameters.name: key, index, or path
parameters.description: An object key, array index, or path element used for extraction.

jsonb.returns: JSON operators return json/jsonb, text, boolean, or a modified jsonb value depending on the operator.

example.title: Store and query jsonb
example.explanation: This stores a JSON document, indexes the jsonb column, extracts a field as text, and finds rows by contained key and value.

useCases.title: Flexible records
useCases.scenario: Store application records with changing fields.

useCases.title: JSON filtering
useCases.scenario: Search documents by keys and values.

useCases.title: Indexed document search
useCases.scenario: Keep a JSON document queryable with an index.

interview.question: How do json and jsonb differ?
interview.answer: json stores the original JSON text, so it preserves whitespace, key order, and duplicate keys. jsonb converts the value to a binary, decomposed form; it usually processes faster and supports indexes.
interview.followUp: Which type is usually better for application data? jsonb, unless the exact input text must be preserved or the application needs json-specific behavior.

interview.question: What does jsonb containment mean?
interview.answer: The @> operator tests whether the left jsonb value contains the right jsonb value. Object structure and values must match, but array order and duplicate array elements do not affect containment.
interview.followUp: Does @> search for a nested object anywhere? No. The structure in the right operand must match the corresponding structure in the left operand.

interview.question: How can jsonb queries use indexes?
interview.answer: A GIN index on a jsonb column can support key-exists, containment, and jsonpath-match operators. The default operator class supports ?, ?|, ?&, @>, @?, and @@.
interview.followUp: Why might an expression index be needed? An index on the whole column may not support an operator applied after extracting a nested value, such as data->'tags' ? 'x'.

keyPoints: Use json or jsonb to store validated JSON instead of plain text.
jsonb converts input into a decomposed form. This adds input work but avoids reparsing during later processing.
jsonb supports indexes, which can make searches over JSON documents efficient.
The -> operator returns a JSON value for an object key or array index. The ->> operator returns text.
Missing keys, indexes, or incompatible JSON structure return SQL NULL when using extraction operators.
Objects are usually better than arrays for many containment or existence checks because PostgreSQL can search them without a linear scan.
gotchas: jsonb changes formatting, key order, and duplicate keys. If a key appears more than once, only the last value remains.
jsonb rejects numbers that PostgreSQL numeric cannot represent. json can accept them as input.
The ? operator checks only the top level. It does not search inside nested objects or arrays.

jsonb_agg.summary: `jsonb_agg` collects values from multiple rows into one JSONB array. It includes nulls and supports ordering inside the aggregate call.
jsonb_agg.explanation: `jsonb_agg` takes one value from each input row and returns one JSONB array. It keeps null values and converts each input with PostgreSQL's JSON conversion rules. The order is not guaranteed unless an `ORDER BY` clause is placed inside the aggregate call.
jsonb_agg.syntax: jsonb_agg ( anyelement ORDER BY input_sort_columns ) → jsonb

parameters.name: anyelement
parameters.description: The value from each input row to convert and append to the JSONB array.

parameters.name: input_sort_columns
parameters.description: Optional expressions that define the order of elements inside the result.

jsonb_agg.returns: A JSONB array containing all input values, including nulls; NULL when there are no input rows.

example.title: Aggregate JSON values
example.code:
SELECT jsonb_agg(value ORDER BY value) AS values
FROM jsonb_array_elements('[3,1,2]'::jsonb) AS item(value);
example.explanation: This expands a JSON array into rows, then collects the values into a JSONB array in sorted order.

useCases.title: Build a JSONB array
useCases.scenario: Return child records or scalar values as one JSONB array for an API query.

useCases.title: Order array elements
useCases.scenario: Preserve a required display or ranking order in the generated array.

useCases.title: Aggregate grouped results
useCases.scenario: Convert grouped SQL results into JSONB for further JSON processing.

interview.question: What does `jsonb_agg` return?
interview.answer: `jsonb_agg(anyelement)` collects all input values, including nulls, into one JSONB array. Each value is converted using the rules for `to_jsonb`.
interview.followUp: How do you omit null values? Use `jsonb_agg_strict`, which skips null inputs.

interview.question: What happens with no input rows?
interview.answer: The aggregate returns NULL when no input rows are selected. It does not return an empty JSONB array automatically.
interview.followUp: How can a query return an empty array instead? Wrap the aggregate with `coalesce`, using an empty JSONB array as the replacement.

interview.question: How do you control array order?
interview.answer: Input order is unspecified by default. Put `ORDER BY` inside the aggregate call when the JSON array must have a defined order.
interview.followUp: Why not rely only on a sorted subquery? An outer query operation, such as a join, can reorder that subquery before aggregation.

keyPoints: The function accepts one value expression and returns a single `jsonb` result.
It puts every input value, including SQL NULL values, into one JSONB array.
PostgreSQL converts each input value using its JSON conversion rules.
It reduces the rows supplied to the aggregate into one result.
gotchas: An empty input produces NULL, not an empty JSON array. Use `coalesce` when an empty array is needed.
Without an inner `ORDER BY`, the array element order is unspecified.

jsonb_build_object.summary: jsonb_build_object creates a JSONB object from alternating key and value arguments. Keys become text, and values use PostgreSQL's JSON conversion rules.
jsonb_build_object.explanation: jsonb_build_object takes alternating keys and values and creates a JSONB object. Keys are converted to text. Values are converted using PostgreSQL's JSON conversion rules, so values can have different SQL types.

parameters.name: VARIADIC "any"
parameters.description: Alternating key and value arguments. Keys are converted to text; values use to_json or to_jsonb conversion.

example.title: Build a JSONB object
example.code: SELECT jsonb_build_object('name', 'Ada', 'active', true);
example.explanation: This returns a JSONB object with two key-value pairs.

useCases.title: Build response objects
useCases.scenario: Create a JSONB response from selected SQL values.

useCases.title: Mix value types
useCases.scenario: Combine values with different SQL types in one object.

useCases.title: Create nested objects
useCases.scenario: Place a row or composite value inside a JSONB object.

interview.question: What does jsonb_build_object do?
interview.answer: It accepts a variadic list of arguments and returns a JSONB value. The arguments are interpreted as alternating keys and values.
interview.followUp: How are the arguments converted? Keys are coerced to text; values are converted as they would be by to_json or to_jsonb.

interview.question: Can its values have different types?
interview.answer: It can create an object from values of different SQL types. For example, text, numbers, booleans, and rows can appear in one call.
interview.followUp: What happens to a row value? PostgreSQL converts it to a JSON object using the row's field names or generated field names.

interview.question: What type does it return?
interview.answer: The function returns jsonb, which is PostgreSQL's binary JSON type. Its signature is jsonb_build_object(VARIADIC "any").
interview.followUp: How does this differ from json_build_object? The corresponding json_build_object function returns the json type instead of jsonb.

keyPoints: The function creates one JSONB object from a variable number of arguments.
Each key becomes text, and each value follows PostgreSQL's JSON conversion rules.
Its signature accepts a variadic any-type argument list and returns jsonb.
A key can come from a non-text value, and a row value can become a nested JSON object.
gotchas: Pass arguments as key, value pairs. An odd or incorrectly ordered argument list does not describe the intended object.
Keys become text, while values use PostgreSQL's JSON conversion rules.

lag.summary: LAG returns a value from an earlier row in the same window partition. It is useful for comparing each row with a previous row.
lag.explanation: LAG evaluates a value at a row before the current row in the same partition. The offset and default are evaluated for the current row. The function needs an OVER clause, and its result depends on the window's ORDER BY.
lag.syntax: lag(value anycompatible [, offset integer [, default anycompatible ]]) → anycompatible

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: Expression whose value is read from an earlier row.

parameters.name: offset
parameters.description: Number of rows before the current row. Defaults to 1.

parameters.name: default
parameters.description: Value returned when the offset row does not exist. Defaults to NULL.

lag.returns: The value of the value expression at the row offset rows before the current row; otherwise the default, or NULL if omitted.

example.title: Find the previous row value
example.code:
SELECT employee_id,
       department_id,
       salary,
       LAG(salary, 1, 0) OVER (
         PARTITION BY department_id
         ORDER BY employee_id
       ) AS previous_salary
FROM employees;
example.explanation: This returns each employee's salary and the salary from the previous row in the same department. It returns 0 when that row does not exist.

useCases.title: Period-over-period comparisons
useCases.scenario: Compare a current value with the value from the previous ordered row.

useCases.title: Sequence analysis
useCases.scenario: Read the previous event, state, or timestamp within each group.

useCases.title: Boundary defaults
useCases.scenario: Supply a known value when an earlier row is unavailable.

interview.question: What does LAG do?
interview.answer: LAG returns the value from a row that is a specified number of rows before the current row within its partition. Its default offset is 1, and its default fallback value is NULL.
interview.followUp: How do you compare rows within groups? Use PARTITION BY in the window definition, then ORDER BY the column that defines row order.

interview.question: Why does LAG need OVER and ORDER BY?
interview.answer: The OVER clause is required because LAG is a window function. PARTITION BY creates independent groups, while ORDER BY determines which row is before the current row.
interview.followUp: What happens if the offset row is missing? LAG returns the supplied default, or NULL if no default is supplied.

interview.question: What are LAG's arguments?
interview.answer: The value expression, offset, and default are evaluated with respect to the current row. The offset is an integer, and the default must be type-compatible with the value.
interview.followUp: Can the offset be greater than one? Yes. Pass the desired number of preceding rows as the offset argument.

keyPoints: LAG reads a value from an earlier row in the current partition.
If you omit the offset, LAG looks one row back. If you omit the default, it returns NULL when no row exists.
The offset and fallback expression use the current row as their reference.
Call LAG with an OVER clause.
Rows with equal ORDER BY values are peers, so use an ordering that gives the needed row sequence.
gotchas: The result depends on the window's ORDER BY. Without a meaningful order, previous and next rows are not defined for your use case.
If the requested earlier row does not exist, LAG returns the default value, or NULL when default is omitted.
The default must have a type compatible with the value expression.

LATERAL.summary: LATERAL lets a FROM subquery or table function use columns from an earlier FROM item. PostgreSQL evaluates it for each source row or row set and joins the results.
LATERAL.explanation: LATERAL lets a subquery or table function use columns from an earlier item in the FROM list. PostgreSQL evaluates the lateral item for each row, or row set, supplied by those earlier items, then joins the produced rows with their source rows.
LATERAL.syntax:
FROM source_table AS s
[INNER | LEFT] JOIN LATERAL (subquery) AS alias ON condition

parameters.name: source columns
parameters.description: The earlier FROM columns referenced by the lateral subquery or function.

LATERAL.returns: Rows from the lateral item joined with the rows that supplied its referenced columns.

example.title: Use LATERAL with a function
example.code:
SELECT m.name, p.name
FROM manufacturers AS m
LEFT JOIN LATERAL get_product_names(m.id) AS p(name)
  ON true;
example.explanation: For each manufacturer, the function receives that manufacturer's id. The left join keeps manufacturers whose function call returns no rows.

useCases.title: Pass row values to a table function
useCases.scenario: A function needs one value from each source row.

useCases.title: Correlated FROM subquery
useCases.scenario: A subquery must calculate rows using columns from an earlier table.

useCases.title: Keep unmatched source rows
useCases.scenario: Rows from the source must remain when the lateral item is empty.

interview.question: What does LATERAL do?
interview.answer: LATERAL allows a FROM subquery or function to reference columns from FROM items placed before it. PostgreSQL evaluates that item for each source row or source row set.
interview.followUp: Why use LEFT JOIN LATERAL? It preserves source rows when the lateral subquery or function produces no rows.

interview.question: Is LATERAL required for table functions?
interview.answer: A table function can use earlier FROM columns in its arguments even without writing LATERAL. Writing the keyword can still make the dependency clearer.
interview.followUp: Does this rule apply to a subquery? No. A subquery needs LATERAL to reference preceding FROM items.

interview.question: How is a lateral item evaluated?
interview.answer: With a cross-reference, PostgreSQL evaluates the lateral item using the current values from the preceding source row or rows. It then joins the resulting rows normally.
interview.followUp: Can a lateral item be inside a join tree? Yes. It can refer to items on the left side of the join where it is on the right side.

keyPoints: Put LATERAL before a subquery in FROM when that subquery must use columns from an earlier FROM item.
LATERAL works directly in the FROM list and inside a join tree.
PostgreSQL evaluates a cross-referencing lateral item once for each source row, or for each source row set.
Rows produced by the lateral item are joined with the source rows that supplied its input.
Use LATERAL when a source column is needed to compute which rows the next FROM item returns.
gotchas: Use LEFT JOIN when you want source rows to remain even if the lateral item returns no rows.
The keyword is optional for table functions because their arguments can already refer to earlier FROM items.
A lateral item that refers to a source must use an INNER or LEFT join with that source.

lead.summary: `lead` returns a value from a later row in the current window partition. It defaults to looking one row ahead and returns `NULL` when that row does not exist.
lead.explanation: `lead` reads a value from a later row in the same window partition. The optional offset says how many rows forward to look, and the optional default is returned when that row does not exist. Both expressions are evaluated for the current row. Use `OVER` to define the window and its ordering.
lead.syntax: lead ( value anycompatible [ , offset integer [ , default anycompatible ] ] ) → anycompatible

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: Expression whose value is read from a later row in the partition.

parameters.name: offset
parameters.description: Number of rows after the current row. Defaults to 1.

parameters.name: default
parameters.description: Value returned when the requested later row does not exist. Defaults to NULL and must be compatible with `value`.

lead.returns: The value of `value` from the row `offset` rows after the current row; otherwise `default`, or `NULL` if omitted.

example.title: Read neighboring rows
example.code:
SELECT empno, salary,
       lag(salary, 1, 0) OVER (ORDER BY empno) AS previous_salary,
       lead(salary) OVER (ORDER BY empno) AS next_salary
FROM empsalary;
example.explanation: This returns each employee's salary together with the previous salary and the next salary in employee-number order.

useCases.title: Read the next row
useCases.scenario: Compare a row with the following row, such as comparing an event with the next event.

useCases.title: Find forward differences
useCases.scenario: Calculate changes between a current value and the value in the following ordered row.

useCases.title: Look ahead within groups
useCases.scenario: Use `PARTITION BY` to perform the lookup separately for each customer, group, or category.

interview.question: What does `lead` do?
interview.answer: `lead` returns an expression's value from a row a chosen number of rows after the current row in the partition. Its default offset is 1, and its default fallback value is `NULL`.
interview.followUp: How can the lookup be grouped? Add `PARTITION BY` in `OVER`; the offset is then applied within each partition.

interview.question: What are the arguments to `lead`?
interview.answer: The signature is `lead(value [, offset [, default ]])`. `value` is the expression to read, `offset` is the number of later rows, and `default` is used when that row is absent.
interview.followUp: What constraint applies to the fallback? The default must have a type compatible with `value`.

interview.question: Why is `OVER` required?
interview.answer: `lead` is a window function, so it must be called with an `OVER` clause. The window ordering determines which rows count as later rows.
interview.followUp: How does this differ from an aggregate window function? An aggregate uses the current row's window frame, while `lead` selects one row at an offset.

keyPoints: `lead` gets a value from a later row in the current partition.
If omitted, `offset` is 1 and the fallback is `NULL`.
The offset and fallback expressions are evaluated for each current row.
The `default` expression must have a type compatible with `value`.
Call `lead` with window syntax and include an `OVER` clause.
gotchas: The last rows may have no later row. In that case, `lead` returns the supplied default, or `NULL` when no default is supplied.
The result depends on the window's `ORDER BY`. Without a stable ordering, the meaning of “next” row can be unclear.

LISTEN.summary: LISTEN subscribes a PostgreSQL session to a notification channel. The session receives events when NOTIFY uses that channel.
LISTEN.explanation: LISTEN subscribes the current database session to a named notification channel. When any session in the same database runs NOTIFY for that channel, PostgreSQL sends the event to every subscribed session, which then passes it to its client application.

parameters.name: channel
parameters.description: Name of the notification channel. It can be any identifier.

example.title: Listen for a notification
example.code:
LISTEN virtual;
NOTIFY virtual;
example.explanation: Run LISTEN to subscribe to the channel, then use NOTIFY to send an event to listeners.

useCases.title: Send application events
useCases.scenario: A database change should signal a waiting application process.

useCases.title: Coordinate database clients
useCases.scenario: Several sessions need updates about a shared database event.

interview.question: What does LISTEN do?
interview.answer: LISTEN registers the current session for a notification channel. A NOTIFY on that channel sends an event to all sessions listening in the same database.
interview.followUp: When does the subscription become active? It becomes active at transaction commit, not when the command is first issued.

interview.question: What happens if LISTEN is run twice for the same channel?
interview.answer: A session can listen to multiple channels by issuing LISTEN for each channel. Repeating LISTEN for a channel that it already watches has no effect.
interview.followUp: How can a session stop receiving events? It uses UNLISTEN for the chosen channel.

interview.question: How does an application detect notifications?
interview.answer: A client must use its PostgreSQL interface to receive events. With libpq, it runs LISTEN as SQL and periodically calls PQnotifies to check for received notifications.
interview.followUp: What setup order avoids the initial race? Commit LISTEN, inspect the database in a new transaction, and then process later notifications.

keyPoints: LISTEN subscribes the current session to the named notification channel.
A matching NOTIFY sends an event to every session currently subscribed to the channel.
The database session passes the notification event to its connected client application.
Use UNLISTEN to remove a session's subscription for a channel.
All channel subscriptions disappear automatically when the database session ends.
gotchas: The subscription is not active until the transaction commits. If the transaction rolls back, the subscription change is undone.
When starting a listener, commit LISTEN first. Then inspect the database in a new transaction before relying on later notifications.

Logical replication.summary: Logical replication copies selected PostgreSQL data from a publisher to subscribers. It starts with existing data, then continuously sends later changes while preserving commit order within a subscription.
Logical replication.explanation: Logical replication copies selected database changes from a publisher to subscribers. It first copies existing table data, then sends later changes as they happen and applies commits in publisher order within one subscription.

example.title: Create a publication and subscription
example.explanation: The publisher exposes the orders table through a publication. The subscriber creates a subscription that pulls changes from that publication.

useCases.title: Incremental replication
useCases.scenario: Send changes from one database to another as they occur.

useCases.title: Data consolidation
useCases.scenario: Build an analytical database from several source databases.

useCases.title: Cross-version or cross-platform replication
useCases.scenario: Move data between different major PostgreSQL versions or operating systems.

useCases.title: Selective data sharing
useCases.scenario: Expose only part of a database to another database or user group.

interview.question: How does PostgreSQL logical replication work?
interview.answer: A publisher defines publications, and a subscriber creates subscriptions to pull data from them. The subscriber first receives an initial snapshot, then receives later changes continuously.
interview.followUp: Can a subscriber publish data again? Yes. A subscriber is a normal PostgreSQL instance, so it can define its own publications.

interview.question: What are the publisher and subscriber roles?
interview.answer: Logical replication uses a publish-and-subscribe model. A publication selects the changes to expose, while a subscription connects to the publisher and applies those changes to local tables.
interview.followUp: What is the main architectural flow? WAL changes are decoded by a walsender, converted by pgoutput, sent through the streaming replication protocol, and applied by an apply worker.

interview.question: How is consistency maintained?
interview.answer: Existing data is copied from a snapshot before ongoing changes are applied. Changes are applied in commit order, which preserves transactional consistency for publications within one subscription.
interview.followUp: What happens when the subscriber also receives local writes? Local or other-subscriber writes can create conflicts with replicated changes.

keyPoints: It can replicate selected data instead of requiring an exact copy of the whole database.
Changes are applied in publisher commit order within a subscription.
A walsender reads the publisher's WAL through logical decoding.
The publication controls which decoded changes are sent.
After decoding, changes are continuously sent to the subscriber.
The subscriber's apply worker maps incoming changes to local tables and applies them.
gotchas: Writes made directly on the subscriber or by other subscribers can conflict with replicated changes.
The apply process does not normally fire subscriber triggers or rules. Table settings can enable them.
Initial synchronization differs from normal apply: it behaves like COPY and fires row and statement INSERT triggers.

MERGE.summary: MERGE conditionally inserts, updates, deletes, or skips rows in a target table using source data. It joins source and target rows, then runs the first matching WHEN action for each candidate row.
MERGE.explanation: MERGE joins source rows with the target table. For each candidate row, it decides whether the row is matched, unmatched in the source, or unmatched in the target. It then runs the first applicable WHEN action, which can insert, update, delete, or do nothing.
MERGE.syntax: [ WITH with_query [, ...] ] MERGE INTO [ ONLY ] target_table_name [ * ] [ [ AS ] target_alias ] USING data_source ON join_condition when_clause [...] [ RETURNING [ WITH ( { OLD | NEW } AS output_alias [, ...] ) ] { * | output_expression [ [ AS ] output_name ] } [, ...] ]

parameters.name: with_query
parameters.description: Optional common table expressions used by the MERGE query.

parameters.name: target_table_name
parameters.description: The table or view to modify.

parameters.name: data_source
parameters.description: The source table or query that supplies rows.

parameters.name: join_condition
parameters.description: A Boolean expression that matches source rows to target rows.

parameters.name: when_clause
parameters.description: An ordered conditional action such as WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE.

MERGE.returns: On success, MERGE returns a command tag in the form MERGE total_count. With RETURNING, it returns values computed for each inserted, updated, or deleted row.

example.title: Add or update inventory
example.code:
MERGE INTO inventory AS i
USING (VALUES ('pen', 10)) AS s(name, quantity)
ON s.name = i.name
WHEN MATCHED THEN
  UPDATE SET quantity = i.quantity + s.quantity
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN
  INSERT (name, quantity)
  VALUES (s.name, s.quantity);
example.explanation: This adds stock for an existing item. It inserts a new item when no target row matches.

useCases.title: Upsert-like data loading
useCases.scenario: Apply incoming records to an existing table.

useCases.title: Data synchronization
useCases.scenario: Remove or change target rows that are missing or present in the source.

useCases.title: Report changed rows
useCases.scenario: Return values for every row changed by the statement.

related: ALTER TABLE ... ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY

interview.question: What does MERGE do?
interview.answer: MERGE combines source data with a target table and conditionally performs one action for each candidate change row. The action is selected from the WHEN clauses in their written order.
