Physical start: START_REPLICATION [SLOT slot_name] PHYSICAL

parameters.name: replication
parameters.description: Startup parameter. `true`, `on`, `yes`, or `1` selects physical mode; `database` selects logical mode.

parameters.name: dbname
parameters.description: Database name used by logical WAL sender mode.

parameters.name: proto_version
parameters.description: Logical protocol version accepted by `pgoutput`; versions 1 through 4 are documented.

parameters.name: publication_names
parameters.description: Comma-separated publications to receive from `pgoutput`.

parameters.name: slot_name
parameters.description: Logical replication slot used by `START_REPLICATION`.

Streaming replication.returns: `IDENTIFY_SYSTEM` returns one row containing the cluster system identifier, timeline, current WAL location, and database name. `CREATE_REPLICATION_SLOT` returns the slot name, consistent WAL point, snapshot name, and output plugin; snapshot and plugin fields are null for physical slots.

example.title: Inspect a replication connection
example.code: psql "dbname=postgres replication=database" -c "IDENTIFY_SYSTEM;"
example.explanation: This opens a logical replication connection and asks the server for its system identity.

useCases.title: Physical standby replication
useCases.scenario: Keep a standby close to the primary by sending WAL as it is generated.

useCases.title: Logical change streaming
useCases.scenario: Send decoded row changes to a subscriber or change-data-capture client.

useCases.title: WAL retention with replication slots
useCases.scenario: Keep required WAL available while a standby or subscriber is temporarily disconnected.

useCases.title: Replication connection testing
useCases.scenario: Inspect the server identity and current WAL position from a replication connection.

interview.question: How does a client select physical or logical replication?
interview.answer: Set `replication=true` in the startup message for physical replication. Set `replication=database` for logical replication, and use the `dbname` startup parameter to select the database. Only the simple query protocol is available in either mode.
interview.followUp: How does logical streaming begin? Use `START_REPLICATION SLOT slot_name LOGICAL` with the required output-plugin options, such as `proto_version` and `publication_names` for `pgoutput`.

interview.question: What is streaming replication and what is its default behavior?
interview.answer: Streaming replication sends WAL records from the primary as they are generated, instead of waiting for a complete WAL file. It is asynchronous by default, so the standby can lag behind the primary.
interview.followUp: How can WAL retention be protected for a standby? Configure a replication slot, set `wal_keep_size`, or keep an accessible WAL archive with enough retained segments.

interview.question: How are logical changes and relation metadata sent?
interview.answer: A logical protocol transaction is surrounded by `Begin` and `Commit` messages. DML messages identify a relation by OID; a `Relation` message supplies its schema before the first DML for that relation, and the client should cache that metadata.
interview.followUp: What happens with a non-built-in column type? A `Type` message arrives before the `Relation` message, so the client should cache and use that type mapping.

keyPoints: Use a true Boolean startup value to enter physical WAL sender mode.
Use `replication=database` to enter logical WAL sender mode.
The standby receives WAL incrementally while the primary generates it.
By default, a commit does not wait for the standby to receive or apply the change.
A replication slot helps retain WAL until the consumer has received it.
gotchas: Replication mode does not support the extended query protocol.
Logical protocol version 2 needs PostgreSQL 14 or newer.
A standby can need a new base backup if required WAL is removed before it receives it.

string_agg.summary: string_agg joins non-null values into one string, placing a delimiter between values. Use an ORDER BY clause inside the aggregate when the order must be controlled.
string_agg.explanation: string_agg receives text values and combines them into one string. It places the delimiter before each value after the first. Add ORDER BY inside the call when the result must follow a defined input order.
string_agg.syntax:
string_agg(value text, delimiter text) → text
string_agg(value bytea, delimiter bytea ORDER BY input_sort_columns) → bytea

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: A text value to include in the result; NULL values are ignored.

parameters.name: delimiter
parameters.description: Text placed between included values.

example.title: Join values in order
example.code:
SELECT string_agg(name, ', ' ORDER BY name)
FROM users;
example.explanation: This joins non-null names with a comma and space, in alphabetical order.

useCases.title: Build a delimited list
useCases.scenario: Create a readable list of names or labels in one result column.

useCases.title: Control concatenation order
useCases.scenario: Produce stable output for reports or tests.

useCases.title: Handle empty input
useCases.scenario: Return a safe empty string when no rows match.

interview.question: What does string_agg do?
interview.answer: string_agg combines non-null input values into one string and places a delimiter between them. It supports text inputs and also a bytea form.
interview.followUp: What happens when the input has no rows? It returns NULL, so COALESCE can replace that with an empty string.

interview.question: How do you control the order of concatenated values?
interview.answer: Write the delimiter as the second argument, then put ORDER BY after all aggregate arguments: string_agg(value, delimiter ORDER BY sort_expression).
interview.followUp: Why not put ORDER BY between the arguments? That changes how PostgreSQL parses the aggregate call and can make the delimiter an ordering expression.

interview.question: How does string_agg handle NULL values?
interview.answer: NULL input values are ignored. The delimiter is placed before each later included value, provided the delimiter is not NULL.
interview.followUp: How can a query return a predictable empty result instead of NULL? Wrap the aggregate with COALESCE, such as COALESCE(string_agg(x, ','), '').

keyPoints: string_agg joins the non-null input values into one string.
The delimiter appears between consecutive included values.
The text form takes a value and a delimiter, and returns text.
A bytea form also exists and returns bytea.
Without an in-aggregate ORDER BY, concatenation order is not guaranteed.
gotchas: string_agg returns NULL when there are no input rows. Use COALESCE if an empty string is needed.
The delimiter is inserted between values, not before the first value. A NULL delimiter is not inserted.
Input order is otherwise unspecified, so put ORDER BY inside string_agg when order matters.

text.summary: PostgreSQL has json and jsonb types for valid JSON. json preserves input text; jsonb uses a decomposed form that is usually faster to query and supports indexing.
text.explanation: PostgreSQL provides json and jsonb for valid JSON data. json keeps the input text, while jsonb converts it to a binary form that is usually faster to process and can use indexes. jsonb removes insignificant whitespace, key order, and duplicate keys.
text.returns: A JSON value stored as json or jsonb; query operators and functions can inspect or extract its contents.

example.title: Store and query jsonb
example.explanation: This stores JSON in jsonb, finds rows by a contained key-value pair, and reads a text value.

useCases.title: Flexible document data
useCases.scenario: Store application records whose fields can change over time.

useCases.title: Document queries
useCases.scenario: Query JSON keys, values, or nested structures.

useCases.title: Indexed jsonb search
useCases.scenario: Speed up containment and existence searches.

interview.question: What is the difference between json and jsonb?
interview.answer: json stores the original JSON text and reparses it during processing. jsonb stores a decomposed binary representation, so input conversion costs more but later processing is usually faster. jsonb also supports indexing.
interview.followUp: When would json be the better choice? Use it when exact input text matters, such as preserving whitespace, key order, or duplicate keys.

interview.question: How does jsonb containment work?
interview.answer: The @> operator tests whether the left jsonb value contains the right value. Containment follows the JSON structure, and arrays can contain primitive values as a special case.
interview.followUp: How can a containment query match nested data without extracting each sub-object? Put the required nested structure in the right-hand JSON value.

interview.question: What does the jsonb existence operator test?
interview.answer: The ? operator checks whether a text string is a top-level object key or array element in a jsonb value. It does not treat object values as matches and does not recurse into nested structures.
interview.followUp: What data shape is better for many existence checks? Objects are better because PostgreSQL optimizes them for searching, unlike arrays that require linear searches.

keyPoints: Use json or jsonb to store valid JSON instead of plain text.
jsonb has extra input conversion work.
jsonb is usually faster for repeated queries because PostgreSQL does not reparse the stored document.
Indexes can make jsonb searches faster.
JSON document structure is usually not enforced by the database, so applications should define a predictable shape.
gotchas: Do not use jsonb when you must preserve formatting, object-key order, or duplicate keys.
A number accepted by general JSON may still fail when converted to jsonb if it exceeds PostgreSQL numeric limits.
The ? operator does not search inside nested objects or arrays.

timestamptz.sourceTitle: PostgreSQL: Documentation: 18: B.2. Handling of Invalid or Ambiguous Timestamps
timestamptz.summary: PostgreSQL accepts local timestamps that fall in daylight-saving gaps or repeats. It resolves them by choosing a UTC offset, but an explicit offset or abbreviation can select the intended instant.
timestamptz.explanation: A `timestamptz` value represents an instant with a time-zone offset. When PostgreSQL parses a local time during a daylight-saving transition, it chooses an offset if the input does not identify one. A skipped spring-forward time uses the offset before the change. A repeated fall-back time uses the offset after the change. You can specify a numeric offset or a matching abbreviation to select an interpretation.

parameters.name: input
parameters.description: A date/time string that PostgreSQL converts to a timestamp with time zone.

parameters.name: offset or abbreviation
parameters.type: numeric UTC offset or time-zone abbreviation
parameters.description: An optional numeric UTC offset or time-zone abbreviation used to identify the intended offset.

timestamptz.returns: A timestamp with time zone, or an error for out-of-range date/time fields.

example.title: Resolve an ambiguous time
example.code:
SELECT '2018-11-04 01:30'::timestamptz;

SELECT '2018-11-04 01:30 EDT'::timestamptz;
example.explanation: The first value uses the standard-time interpretation. Adding EDT selects the earlier daylight-time interpretation.

useCases.title: Parse local times
useCases.scenario: Convert user-entered local date/time values while handling daylight-saving transitions.

useCases.title: Disambiguate repeated times
useCases.scenario: Select one of the two instants represented by a repeated clock time.

useCases.title: Provide an explicit offset
useCases.scenario: Store or inspect a timestamp with a known offset.

interview.question: How does PostgreSQL parse an ambiguous local timestamp during a fall-back transition?
interview.answer: PostgreSQL normally chooses the standard-time interpretation when a local timestamp is ambiguous. During a fall-back transition, it uses the offset that applies after the clock moves back.
interview.followUp: How do you choose the other occurrence? Include a daylight-saving abbreviation such as `EDT`, or provide an explicit numeric UTC offset.

interview.question: What happens when a timestamp falls in a daylight-saving spring-forward gap?
interview.answer: A local time inside a spring-forward gap is accepted rather than rejected. PostgreSQL applies the offset from just before the transition, then displays the resulting instant using the new offset.
interview.followUp: What is the safest way to avoid relying on this inference? Include an explicit UTC offset or a time-zone abbreviation in the input.

interview.question: How can an input specify the intended UTC offset?
interview.answer: An explicit numeric UTC offset or a time-zone abbreviation can identify the intended instant. This avoids relying on PostgreSQL's inference when the zone's offset changes.
interview.followUp: Does the default rule apply to every time zone? No. It applies when PostgreSQL must infer an offset for a zone whose offset varies.

keyPoints: Daylight-saving changes can create local times that either never occurred or occurred twice.
PostgreSQL accepts these cases and resolves them by choosing a UTC offset.
A syntactically valid date with an impossible field value raises an error.
A daylight-saving abbreviation can force the alternate interpretation of a repeated local time.
An explicit numeric offset or suitable abbreviation can remove uncertainty from the input.
gotchas: A repeated local time defaults to the offset after the clock moves back. Add an abbreviation or numeric offset when you need the other instant.
A local time skipped by a spring-forward change is not rejected. PostgreSQL maps it using the offset that existed before the jump.

to_tsquery.summary: to_tsquery converts a structured text query into a tsquery value. It normalizes words, removes stop words, and supports operators, weights, and prefix matching.
to_tsquery.explanation: to_tsquery parses a query string into PostgreSQL's tsquery type. The input must use valid tsquery operators such as &, |, !, and <->. Each token is normalized with the chosen text search configuration, and stop words are removed.
to_tsquery.syntax: to_tsquery([ config regconfig, ] querytext text) returns tsquery

parameters.name: config
parameters.description: Text search configuration used to normalize tokens. If omitted, PostgreSQL uses the default configuration.

parameters.name: querytext
parameters.description: Query text containing tokens and valid tsquery operators.

example.title: Create a normalized query
example.code: SELECT to_tsquery('english', 'The & Fat & Rats');
example.explanation: This creates a query containing the normalized lexemes fat and rat.

useCases.title: Operator-based search
useCases.scenario: Build a structured search query when the application controls or validates the query syntax.

useCases.title: Weighted fields
useCases.scenario: Limit matches to terms stored with selected tsvector weights.

useCases.title: Prefix search
useCases.scenario: Match words that begin with a given lexeme prefix.

interview.question: What does to_tsquery do?
interview.answer: to_tsquery converts text into a tsquery after normalizing each token with a text search configuration. The input must already use valid tsquery operators.
interview.followUp: How would you accept raw user input safely? Use websearch_to_tsquery, which supports simpler syntax and does not raise syntax errors.

interview.question: Which operators can appear in a to_tsquery input?
interview.answer: Use & for AND, | for OR, ! for NOT, and <-> for an adjacent phrase relationship. Parentheses can group parts of the query.
interview.followUp: How can a query require a prefix? Add * to a lexeme, such as supern:*.

interview.question: What are weight and prefix labels used for?
interview.answer: A weight label restricts a lexeme to matching tsvector entries with selected weights, such as :AB. A trailing * requests prefix matching for that lexeme.
interview.followUp: What must be done before searching? Convert the document with to_tsvector, then test it with the @@ match operator.

keyPoints: to_tsquery returns a tsquery value from a query string.
The main operators are &, |, !, and <->.
Each token becomes a normalized lexeme using the supplied configuration or the default one.
Stop words are omitted according to the selected configuration.
A star enables prefix matching for a lexeme.
gotchas: The input is strict. Tokens must be separated by valid operators, or PostgreSQL raises a syntax error.
The function normalizes words and removes configured stop words, so its result may differ from the original input.

to_tsvector.summary: to_tsvector converts document text into a searchable tsvector. It normalizes words, removes stop words, and records lexeme positions using a text search configuration.
to_tsvector.explanation: to_tsvector parses document text according to a text search configuration. It turns tokens into normalized lexemes, removes tokens such as stop words, and records lexeme positions. The resulting tsvector can be matched with a tsquery using @@.
to_tsvector.syntax: to_tsvector([ config regconfig, ] document text) returns tsvector

parameters.name: config
parameters.description: Optional text search configuration used to parse and normalize the document.

parameters.name: document
parameters.description: Document text to parse.

example.title: Create a document vector
example.code: SELECT to_tsvector('english', 'A fat cat ate rats');
example.explanation: This parses English text, removes stop words, and normalizes word forms into a searchable tsvector.

useCases.title: Index document text
useCases.scenario: Build a searchable representation of article text before matching it with a tsquery.

useCases.title: Search structured documents
useCases.scenario: Combine title, keywords, abstract, and body into one weighted vector for relevance ranking.

useCases.title: Apply language rules
useCases.scenario: Use a language-specific configuration so word forms are normalized for that language.

interview.question: What does to_tsvector do?
interview.answer: to_tsvector converts document text into a tsvector. It parses tokens, normalizes them into lexemes, and stores their positions. The selected text search configuration controls this process.
interview.followUp: Why can a document match a query for “rat” when it contains “rats”? The configuration can normalize both forms to the same lexeme.

interview.question: How does configuration affect the result?
interview.answer: A configuration selects the parser, dictionaries, and token types used during processing. You can pass a configuration explicitly, or PostgreSQL uses the default configuration.
interview.followUp: How would you use different languages? Pass the appropriate regconfig, such as a language-specific configuration, when building the vector.

interview.question: Why use setweight with to_tsvector?
interview.answer: setweight labels lexemes with A, B, C, or D. Concatenating weighted vectors lets an application mark fields such as a title and body for later relevance ranking.
interview.followUp: How can NULL fields be handled in a structured document? Apply coalesce to each field before calling to_tsvector.

keyPoints: The function parses text into tokens and reduces them to normalized lexemes.
The returned tsvector includes positions for its lexemes.
You can choose the configuration, or PostgreSQL uses the default one.
Stop words are ignored because they are often too common to help search.
setweight can mark entries with weights A, B, C, or D.
gotchas: A NULL document produces NULL. Use coalesce when a source column may be NULL.
Do not cast raw text directly to tsvector when you need stemming or other normalization. Use to_tsvector instead.

TRUNCATE.summary: TRUNCATE removes all rows from one or more PostgreSQL tables without scanning them. It immediately reclaims table space and can reset owned sequences or include foreign-key-dependent tables.
TRUNCATE.explanation: TRUNCATE removes every row without scanning the table. It releases the table's disk space immediately. You can include child tables, reset owned sequences, and handle foreign-key dependents with CASCADE. The command takes a strong table lock and can be rolled back inside a transaction.
TRUNCATE.syntax: TRUNCATE [ TABLE ] [ ONLY ] name [ * ] [, ... ] [ RESTART IDENTITY | CONTINUE IDENTITY ] [ CASCADE | RESTRICT ]

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: Table name, optionally including its schema. Use ONLY to exclude descendant tables; * explicitly includes descendants.

parameters.name: RESTART IDENTITY
parameters.description: Reset sequences owned by columns of the truncated tables.

parameters.name: CONTINUE IDENTITY
parameters.description: Leave sequence values unchanged. This is the default.

parameters.name: CASCADE
parameters.description: Include tables with foreign-key references to the target tables.

parameters.name: RESTRICT
parameters.description: Reject the command when unlisted foreign-key referencing tables exist. This is the default.

TRUNCATE.returns: No row set; the command truncates the selected tables.

example.title: Clear a staging table
example.code: TRUNCATE TABLE staging_orders RESTART IDENTITY CASCADE;
example.explanation: Removes all rows from staging_orders, resets sequences owned by its columns, and also truncates tables that reference it with foreign keys.

useCases.title: Empty bulk-load tables
useCases.scenario: Clear a large staging or temporary table after processing while reclaiming its space immediately.

useCases.title: Reset generated IDs
useCases.scenario: Remove a complete dataset and reset its owned identity sequences for the next load.

useCases.title: Truncate related tables
useCases.scenario: Clear a group of related tables when their foreign-key dependencies are known and intended.

interview.question: How does TRUNCATE differ from DELETE?
interview.answer: TRUNCATE removes all rows without scanning the table, so it is usually faster than an unrestricted DELETE. It also reclaims the table's disk space immediately, without a later VACUUM.
interview.followUp: When might DELETE be safer? DELETE supports row-level filtering and fires ON DELETE triggers, while TRUNCATE does neither.

interview.question: What do RESTART IDENTITY and CONTINUE IDENTITY do?
interview.answer: RESTART IDENTITY resets sequences owned by columns of the truncated tables. CONTINUE IDENTITY leaves sequence values unchanged and is the default.
interview.followUp: Are sequence resets reversible? Yes. The implied sequence restart operations are transactional and roll back if the surrounding transaction does not commit.

interview.question: How do CASCADE and RESTRICT affect foreign keys?
interview.answer: RESTRICT is the default and refuses the operation when unlisted tables have foreign-key references to the target. CASCADE includes those referencing tables automatically.
interview.followUp: What happens with partitions? A truncated partition's sibling partitions stay unchanged, but cascading still includes referencing tables and their partitions.

keyPoints: It empties one or more tables in one command.
It avoids reading every row, which makes it useful for large tables.
The freed table space does not require a later VACUUM operation.
Use ONLY to exclude descendant tables; without it, descendants are included.
The caller needs TRUNCATE privilege on every table affected by the operation.
A transaction rollback restores the truncated table data.
gotchas: The command blocks all other concurrent operations on each table until the lock is released.
ON DELETE triggers do not run. ON TRUNCATE triggers do run.
A concurrent transaction using an older snapshot can see the table as empty after truncation.
CASCADE can truncate foreign-key referencing tables automatically, so use it only when all affected tables are intended.

tsvector.summary: PostgreSQL full-text search uses tsvector for searchable documents and tsquery for search expressions. Convert raw text with the parsing functions, then use @@ to test for matches.
tsvector.explanation: PostgreSQL uses tsvector for a normalized, searchable document and tsquery for a normalized search expression. Convert source text with to_tsvector and query text with a query parser, then use @@ to test for a match.
tsvector.syntax: to_tsvector([ config regconfig, ] document text) returns tsvector; to_tsquery([ config regconfig, ] querytext text) returns tsquery; tsvector @@ tsquery

parameters.name: config
parameters.description: Text search configuration used to parse and normalize the input.

parameters.name: document
parameters.description: Document text to convert into a searchable vector.

parameters.name: querytext
parameters.description: Query text containing search terms and supported operators.

tsvector.returns: to_tsvector returns tsvector. to_tsquery, plainto_tsquery, phraseto_tsquery, and websearch_to_tsquery return tsquery. @@ returns boolean.

example.title: Match a document with a query
example.code: SELECT to_tsvector('english', 'PostgreSQL stores searchable text') @@ to_tsquery('english', 'search');
example.explanation: This converts document text and a query into text-search values, then checks whether the document matches.

useCases.title: Document matching
useCases.scenario: Search normalized words in document text.

useCases.title: Phrase search
useCases.scenario: Require words to occur in a specific order or distance.

useCases.title: Weighted fields
useCases.scenario: Give title terms more influence during ranking.

useCases.title: Prefix search
useCases.scenario: Match words that start with a supplied prefix.

interview.question: What are tsvector and tsquery?
interview.answer: tsvector is a sorted list of distinct, normalized lexemes for a document. tsquery stores normalized search terms and combines them with operators such as AND, OR, NOT, and FOLLOWED BY.
interview.followUp: How do you preserve document structure? Use setweight on parts such as a title and body, then merge them with the tsvector concatenation operator ||.

interview.question: How are documents and queries prepared?
interview.answer: to_tsvector parses document text, removes or normalizes tokens according to a text search configuration, and records lexeme positions. to_tsquery parses and normalizes a query while retaining query operators.
interview.followUp: Which function creates a simple AND query from plain user text? plainto_tsquery; for ordered terms, use phraseto_tsquery.

interview.question: How does PostgreSQL perform a full-text match?
interview.answer: The @@ operator returns true when a tsvector document matches a tsquery. FOLLOWED BY checks order and position; <1> means adjacent terms, while larger distances allow intervening lexemes.
interview.followUp: How can matching documents be ordered? Use ts_rank for matching-term frequency or ts_rank_cd when proximity should affect the score.

keyPoints: tsvector stores unique lexemes in sorted order.
Use tsvector as the searchable representation of a document.
tsquery supports AND, OR, and NOT expressions.
Use FOLLOWED BY for terms that must occur in order.
Use @@ to test whether a document matches a query.
Add * to a query lexeme for prefix matching.
gotchas: Casting text directly to tsvector does not normalize words. Use to_tsvector for raw document text.
A NULL input produces a NULL vector, so use coalesce when a source field may be NULL.
plainto_tsquery treats operators, weights, and prefix markers as ordinary input rather than query syntax.

unnest.sourceTitle: PostgreSQL: Documentation: 18: 9.19. Array Functions and Operators
unnest.summary: PostgreSQL's unnest function expands array elements into rows. It can also expand multiple arrays together and optionally add row numbers.
unnest.explanation: unnest turns an array into rows. In the FROM clause, it can accept several arrays and return one column per array; shorter arrays receive NULL values for missing positions. WITH ORDINALITY can add a row number.
unnest.syntax:
unnest(anyarray) → setof anyelement
unnest(anyarray, anyarray [, ...]) → setof anyelement, anyelement [, ...]

parameters.name: anyarray
parameters.description: An array whose elements should become rows.

parameters.name: anyarray, anyarray [, ...]
parameters.description: One or more arrays to expand together in the FROM clause.

unnest.returns: For one array, a set of rows with one element value per row. For multiple arrays, a set of rows with one column per array; shorter arrays are padded with NULL.

example.title: Expand two arrays
example.explanation: This returns one row for each position. The shorter first array supplies NULL for the missing third number.

useCases.title: Query array elements
useCases.scenario: Turn stored array values into rows for filtering or joining.

useCases.title: Pair array values
useCases.scenario: Expand related arrays into aligned columns in a FROM clause.

useCases.title: Track element positions
useCases.scenario: Keep each expanded row's position with WITH ORDINALITY.

interview.question: What does unnest do?
interview.answer: unnest expands an array into a set of rows, with elements read in storage order. For example, ARRAY[1,2] produces two rows.
interview.followUp: How can several arrays be expanded together? Use the multi-array form in FROM; PostgreSQL returns one column for each array and pads shorter arrays with NULL.

interview.question: How do you expand multiple arrays into columns?
interview.answer: Pass multiple arrays to unnest in the FROM clause. The result has a column for each input array, and rows are matched by position.
interview.followUp: What happens when lengths differ? The shorter input is padded with NULL values.

interview.question: What does WITH ORDINALITY add?
interview.answer: WITH ORDINALITY adds a bigint column that numbers result rows from 1. You can rename that column with an AS clause.
interview.followUp: Where can the ordinal value be useful? It can preserve or expose each element's position while processing the expanded rows.

keyPoints: A single array becomes one result row per element.
Element order follows the array's storage order.
Several arrays can be expanded together, even when their element types differ.
WITH ORDINALITY adds a bigint column containing the result row number.
The added row number starts at 1 and increases for each result row.
gotchas: The multi-array form must be used in the query's FROM clause.

UPDATE.summary: UPDATE changes selected columns in rows that meet a condition. It can calculate values from existing columns, other tables, or subqueries, and can return results with RETURNING.
UPDATE.explanation: PostgreSQL UPDATE changes selected columns in rows that meet a condition. Values can use the row's old values, a default, a subquery, or columns from tables in FROM. RETURNING can produce values from each updated row.
UPDATE.syntax: [ WITH [ RECURSIVE ] with_query [, ...] ] UPDATE [ ONLY ] table_name [ * ] [ [ AS ] alias ] SET { column_name = { expression | DEFAULT } | ( column_name [, ...] ) = [ ROW ] ( { expression | DEFAULT } [, ...] ) | ( column_name [, ...] ) = ( sub-SELECT ) } [, ...] [ FROM from_item [, ...] ] [ WHERE condition | WHERE CURRENT OF cursor_name ] [ RETURNING [ WITH ( { OLD | NEW } AS output_alias [, ...] ) ] { * | output_expression [ [ AS ] output_name ] } [, ...] ]

parameters.name: table_name
parameters.description: The table whose rows will be changed.

parameters.name: SET
parameters.description: Columns and expressions that supply new values.

parameters.name: condition
parameters.description: A Boolean expression selecting rows; omitted means all rows.

parameters.name: from_item
parameters.description: Optional tables that provide values for expressions and conditions.

parameters.name: output_expression
parameters.description: Optional expressions returned for each updated row.

UPDATE.returns: On success, UPDATE returns UPDATE count. With RETURNING, it returns one result row for each row updated.

example.title: Update matching rows
example.code:
UPDATE products
SET price = price * 1.10
WHERE price = 5
RETURNING id, price;
example.explanation: Raises the price of matching products and returns the new id and price for each changed row.

useCases.title: Update a subset
useCases.scenario: Change values for rows selected by a condition.

useCases.title: Apply a calculation
useCases.scenario: Compute a new value from the current value.

useCases.title: Use related data
useCases.scenario: Copy values from another table or query.

useCases.title: Return updated data
useCases.scenario: Get changed rows back to the application.

interview.question: What does UPDATE do?
interview.answer: UPDATE names the target table, SET supplies new expressions, and WHERE selects rows. Without WHERE, every row is updated.
interview.followUp: How can an update use another table? Use a subquery or add a FROM clause, while ensuring each target row has at most one source match.

interview.question: Can SET use the old column value?
interview.answer: A SET expression can refer to existing values in the row, so calculations such as price = price * 1.10 are allowed. Columns not listed in SET keep their values.
interview.followUp: What happens when a subquery assignment returns no row? PostgreSQL assigns NULL to the target columns.

interview.question: What is RETURNING used for?
interview.answer: RETURNING computes and returns expressions for rows actually updated. By default, unqualified output uses new values; OLD can request values from before the update.
interview.followUp: What does UPDATE return without RETURNING? It returns a command tag such as UPDATE count, where count is the number of updated rows.

keyPoints: Use UPDATE to change selected columns in every row that satisfies the condition.
Columns missing from SET keep their previous values.
SET expressions may calculate a new value from existing column values.
ONLY prevents updates to child tables that inherit from the target table.
RETURNING sends computed values for each updated row to the client.
The user needs UPDATE permission on the table or the columns being changed.
gotchas: With FROM, each target row should match at most one source row. Multiple matches make the chosen source row unpredictable.
Leaving out WHERE updates every row, so use it only when that is intentional.
The command tag counts matched rows even when the assigned values stay the same.

uuid.summary: PostgreSQL's uuid type stores 128-bit universally unique identifiers. It accepts standard and alternate text forms, and PostgreSQL can generate UUIDv4 and UUIDv7 values.
uuid.explanation: The uuid type stores a 128-bit universally unique identifier. PostgreSQL accepts the standard hexadecimal form and several alternate input forms, and it can generate UUIDv4 and UUIDv7 values in the database.
uuid.returns: A uuid column stores a 128-bit UUID value.

example.title: Create a UUID key
example.explanation: This creates a UUID column, generates a value when an insert omits the column, and reads the stored value.

useCases.title: Distributed identifiers
useCases.scenario: Use a key that can be created by different services without coordinating a database sequence.

useCases.title: External UUID values
useCases.scenario: Store identifiers created by an application or another system.

useCases.title: Database-generated identifiers
useCases.scenario: Use UUIDv4 or UUIDv7 generation supported by PostgreSQL.

interview.question: What does PostgreSQL's uuid type store?
interview.answer: uuid stores a 128-bit UUID. Its standard text form has 32 hexadecimal digits arranged as groups of 8, 4, 4, 4, and 12, with hyphens.
interview.followUp: What other input forms are accepted? PostgreSQL also accepts uppercase digits and the standard form inside braces, among other alternatives.

interview.question: How can UUID values be generated?
interview.answer: A UUID is generated by an algorithm designed to make collisions very unlikely. PostgreSQL has built-in generation for UUID version 4 and version 7, while other algorithms can generate values outside the database.
interview.followUp: Can uuid store a value generated elsewhere? Yes. The type can store any UUID, regardless of where it came from or which version it uses.

interview.question: What is the standard UUID text format?
interview.answer: A UUID is 128 bits, so its standard representation contains 32 hexadecimal digits. The digits are written in five hyphen-separated groups: 8-4-4-4-12.
interview.followUp: Does the text format change the stored size? No. The formatted text represents the same 128-bit identifier.

keyPoints: The uuid type stores universally unique identifiers defined by current UUID standards.
Each UUID is a 128-bit value produced by an algorithm.
PostgreSQL can generate UUID version 4 and version 7 values without an external generator.
The usual display uses lowercase hexadecimal digits separated into groups by hyphens.
The standard group sizes are 8-4-4-4-12, for 32 hexadecimal digits in total.
gotchas: A uuid column accepts UUIDs from different algorithms and versions, not only values generated by PostgreSQL.
UUIDs are useful across distributed systems because their uniqueness is not limited to one database.

VACUUM.summary: VACUUM removes obsolete row versions and makes their space reusable. It can also update planner statistics, maintain visibility information, and freeze old rows to prevent transaction ID wraparound.
VACUUM.explanation: VACUUM removes outdated row versions and makes their space reusable. It can also update planner statistics, maintain the visibility map, and freeze old rows to prevent transaction ID wraparound. Standard VACUUM works while normal reads and writes continue; VACUUM FULL rewrites the table and takes an exclusive lock.

parameters.name: FULL
parameters.description: Rewrites the table to reclaim more disk space; slower and requires an exclusive lock.

parameters.name: FREEZE
parameters.description: Aggressively freezes old row versions.

parameters.name: VERBOSE
parameters.description: Prints detailed vacuum activity reports.

parameters.name: ANALYZE
parameters.description: Updates query-planner statistics after vacuuming.

parameters.name: DISABLE_PAGE_SKIPPING
parameters.description: Skips pages that VACUUM would normally skip.

parameters.name: SKIP_LOCKED
parameters.description: Skips relations that cannot be locked immediately.

parameters.name: INDEX_CLEANUP
parameters.description: Controls whether dead index entries are cleaned up: AUTO, ON, or OFF.

parameters.name: PARALLEL
parameters.description: Runs index vacuum and cleanup phases with background workers.

parameters.name: table_and_columns
parameters.description: Specifies one or more tables, materialized views, and optional columns.

VACUUM.returns: No data value is returned. With VERBOSE, VACUUM emits progress messages and table statistics.

example.title: Vacuum and analyze one table
example.code: VACUUM (VERBOSE, ANALYZE) onek;
example.explanation: This cleans the table, updates planner statistics, and prints detailed progress information.

useCases.title: Reuse space from dead rows
useCases.scenario: A table receives regular updates or deletes.

useCases.title: Refresh planner statistics
useCases.scenario: Queries use outdated estimates for row counts or value distributions.

useCases.title: Prevent transaction ID wraparound
useCases.scenario: A table has many old rows and transaction IDs are advancing.

useCases.title: Reclaim space with VACUUM FULL
useCases.scenario: A table needs physical shrinking after most of its rows were removed.

interview.question: What is the difference between VACUUM and VACUUM FULL?
interview.answer: Standard VACUUM removes dead row versions and marks their space for reuse. It normally does not return that space to the operating system.
interview.followUp: When is VACUUM FULL appropriate? Use it when a table has substantial internal free space and must physically shrink; it rewrites the table and takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock.

interview.question: What does VACUUM ANALYZE do?
interview.answer: VACUUM ANALYZE first performs vacuuming and then collects statistics for the query planner. It is useful in routine maintenance scripts.
interview.followUp: Does autovacuum analyze every special table type? No. It does not automatically analyze foreign tables or partitioned tables, so manual ANALYZE may be needed.

interview.question: How does VACUUM prevent transaction ID wraparound?
interview.answer: Vacuuming freezes sufficiently old row versions. This keeps old transaction IDs from appearing new after the limited transaction ID space wraps around.
interview.followUp: Why must all databases be maintained? Transaction ID protection applies across the cluster, so each database needs regular vacuuming.

keyPoints: VACUUM removes storage used by obsolete or deleted row versions.
Standard VACUUM makes freed space available for later rows but usually keeps the table file the same size.
VACUUM ANALYZE combines cleanup with planner-statistics collection.
The visibility map lets later vacuum runs skip clean pages and can support index-only scans.
Regular vacuuming of every table protects the cluster from transaction ID wraparound.
With no table list, VACUUM processes all permitted tables and materialized views in the current database.
gotchas: VACUUM FULL blocks other use of the table while it runs and needs extra disk space for a new table copy.
Run VACUUM as a standalone command, not inside BEGIN and COMMIT.
Vacuuming can slow other active sessions because it creates heavy I/O traffic.

WITH.sourceTitle: PostgreSQL: Documentation: 18: 7.8. WITH Queries (Common Table Expressions)
WITH.summary: WITH defines named subqueries for use in one larger SQL statement. It can simplify complex queries, support recursion, and include data-changing statements.
WITH.explanation: WITH defines one or more named auxiliary queries for a larger statement. These queries act like temporary tables for that statement. A later query can read their results by name. WITH can also be recursive, and it can contain data-changing statements when their output is returned.

parameters.name: RECURSIVE
parameters.description: Optional keyword that permits recursive self-reference in a SELECT CTE.

parameters.name: with_query
parameters.description: One or more named auxiliary queries, each written as a query expression.

parameters.name: column_name
parameters.description: Optional output column names for the CTE.

parameters.name: MATERIALIZED / NOT MATERIALIZED
parameters.description: Controls whether a qualifying CTE is separately calculated or merged into the parent query.

WITH.returns: A temporary, statement-scoped relation containing the CTE query's output.

example.title: Use a named query
example.code:
WITH regional_sales AS (
  SELECT region, SUM(amount) AS total_sales
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY region
)
SELECT region, total_sales
FROM regional_sales
WHERE total_sales > 1000;
example.explanation: The named query computes totals first. The main query then filters those totals.

useCases.title: Organize complex queries
useCases.scenario: Break a long query into named stages that are easier to read and reuse.

useCases.title: Run recursive queries
useCases.scenario: Walk through tree or graph data with a query that refers to its own output.

useCases.title: Combine data changes and reads
useCases.scenario: Return rows changed by an INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, or MERGE to the main query.

interview.question: What is a common table expression?
interview.answer: A CTE is a named auxiliary query attached to a larger SQL statement. It exists only for that statement and can be referenced like a temporary table.
interview.followUp: How can you control optimization? A side-effect-free CTE used once is normally folded; MATERIALIZED forces separate calculation, while NOT MATERIALIZED forces merging.

interview.question: How does recursive WITH work?
interview.answer: RECURSIVE lets a CTE refer to its own output. Its usual form has a non-recursive term, UNION or UNION ALL, and a recursive term.
interview.followUp: How do you stop cycles? Use UNION when duplicate complete rows are enough, or use CYCLE to track selected columns and stop recursive expansion.

interview.question: Can a WITH query change data?
interview.answer: A data-modifying CTE can be INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, or MERGE. Include RETURNING when the main query needs to read the rows produced by that operation.
interview.followUp: What if RETURNING is omitted? The operation still runs, but it produces no table-like output for the main query to reference.

keyPoints: WITH lets you split a complex statement into named parts.
A CTE may contain a SELECT or a data-changing statement.
RECURSIVE enables a query to use rows produced by its earlier iterations.
A recursive CTE must have a starting term followed by UNION or UNION ALL and a recursive term.
A side-effect-free, non-recursive CTE used once is normally folded into its parent query.
gotchas: Without RECURSIVE, a CTE cannot refer to a later sibling CTE.
Changes made by a data-modifying CTE are not visible elsewhere except through its RETURNING output.
NOT MATERIALIZED can make the CTE run more than once when the parent query uses it multiple times.

Write-ahead log.summary: Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) records database changes before PostgreSQL writes the changed table and index pages. After a crash, PostgreSQL can replay the records to recover changes that were not yet written.
Write-ahead log.explanation: PostgreSQL writes WAL records describing data changes to durable storage before it writes the changed table or index pages. After a crash, recovery replays records for changes that did not reach those pages. This lets commits avoid flushing every changed data page and reduces disk writes.
Write-ahead log.syntax: WAL records are created automatically by PostgreSQL; applications do not call a WAL command directly.

example.title: A transaction protected by WAL
example.explanation: PostgreSQL records the transaction changes in WAL before the changed table pages must be written. After a crash, recovery can replay those records.

useCases.title: Recover committed changes
useCases.scenario: A server crashes after a transaction commits but before all changed data pages reach disk.

useCases.title: Reduce commit-time disk writes
useCases.scenario: A transaction changes many table or index pages.

useCases.title: Maintain data integrity efficiently
useCases.scenario: A database needs reliable crash recovery without flushing every data page on each commit.

interview.question: What is WAL, and how does it protect committed data?
interview.answer: WAL means Write-Ahead Logging. PostgreSQL records changes in the WAL and flushes those records before relying on the changed data pages. If a crash occurs, recovery can replay the records to restore changes.
interview.followUp: Why does WAL reduce writes? Recovery can replay WAL records, so PostgreSQL does not need to flush every changed data page at each commit. The WAL must be flushed instead.

interview.question: Why can PostgreSQL avoid writing all changed data pages at commit?
interview.answer: A transaction commit can avoid flushing every modified table and index page. Once the required WAL records are on permanent storage, recovery can redo changes that were not yet written to data pages.
interview.followUp: What recovery method is this? It is roll-forward recovery, also called REDO, because recovery reapplies logged changes.

interview.question: What does WAL provide during crash recovery?
interview.answer: WAL is a standard method for data integrity. It keeps a durable record of changes so crash recovery can reconstruct database-file contents.
interview.followUp: Does WAL make a journaled file system mandatory? No. The documentation says WAL already provides reliable storage protection, while journaling may still improve boot speed after a crash.

keyPoints: WAL protects database integrity by recording changes before PostgreSQL writes the related table and index pages.
The relevant WAL records must reach permanent storage before PostgreSQL can safely depend on the data-file changes.
After a crash, PostgreSQL can use WAL to recover changes that were not yet applied to database pages.
Recovery replays missing data-page changes from WAL records.
The recovery process is called roll-forward recovery, or REDO.
WAL reduces commit-time disk work because flushing the WAL can be enough to guarantee a commit.
gotchas: WAL ordering matters: changed table and index pages must be written only after their WAL records are logged.
A journaled file system is not required for reliable storage when PostgreSQL WAL is used, although journaling can improve crash-restart boot speed.
